#194289. Think Your Saddle Is Too High? The Signs Every Cyclist Should Know Before Their Next Ride

Think Your Saddle Is Too High? The Signs Every Cyclist Should Know Before Their Next Ride

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1166 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A too-high saddle can feel fast for 10 minutes and terrible for the next two hours.
  • According to recent reports, and because saddle height is the foundation of bike fit, getting it wrong can send you chasing the wrong fix.
  • To get the most out of your ride, consider a full bike fit—not just a saddle height change.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A too-high saddle can feel fast for 10 minutes and terrible for the next two hours. It can show up as pain behind the knee, pressure in the saddle, numbness, or that familiar feeling that you’re reaching for the pedal instead of driving through it.

According to recent reports, and because saddle height is the foundation of bike fit, getting it wrong can send you chasing the wrong fix. Riders often blame the saddle itself, their bib shorts, or even their flexibility when the issue is simply that the seat is a little too high.

To get the most out of your ride, consider a full bike fit—not just a saddle height change. Check out Bicycling’s Guide to the Perfect Bike Fit.

That noted, saddle height is also where fit advice gets messy. There isn’t one perfect number that works for everyone, and the usual rules of thumb are only starting points. Your ideal height depends on your body, your mobility, your injury history, your cleat setup, and more.

Quick Signs Your Saddle May Be Too High• Pain behind the knee • Saddle sores or numbness • Discomfort where your hamstrings meet your glutes • Rocking hips while pedaling • Reaching for the pedal at the bottom of the stroke Quick Fix• Lower the saddle a few millimeters, do a real ride, and reassess.

Here’s how to tell whether your saddle may be too high and a simple at-home check you can do before your next ride.

Saddle height is one of the first things riders adjust, and for good reason. When it’s close, you feel smoother and more comfortable. When it’s off, the problems can spread everywhere.

Sources indicate that but this is where people get tripped up: saddle height is key, but it is only one element in an interconnected system. If your cleats are in the wrong place, your saddle is too far forward or back, or your crankarms don’t suit you, changing saddle height alone may not solve much. It’s the beginning of fit, not the whole thing.

Recent findings suggest that A common starting point is a height that provides around 30 degrees of knee bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke (6 o’clock position). But that is a starting point only, not gospel. Two riders with the same height and inseam may still end up at different saddle heights because bodies aren’t identical and neither are pedaling styles.

In a recent development, pain is the clearest warning that something in your position needs attention. Riding is hard. Suffering through an interval is one thing. Pain caused by pressure, strain, or repeated irritation from a bad setup is another.

A saddle that’s too high often demonstrates up in a few predictable ways:.

This is the classic one. If you feel pain at the back of the knee, especially after longer rides or harder efforts, a too-high saddle is one possible cause.

But not the only one. Fit problems tend to overlap. So treat this as a clue, not a verdict.

If the back of your pedal stroke feels strained, tight, or tuggy, especially when you’re trying to make power, your saddle may be a little high.+.

In a recent development, A high saddle can make you unstable on the bike. Instead of sitting planted, you start shifting and searching. That extra motion can increase friction and pressure, which can mean hot spots, sores, and numbness.

If your hips are dropping side to side at the bottom of the pedal stroke, there’s a decent chance you’re compensating for too much saddle height.

Industry observers note that some riders point their toes naturally. But if you’re really reaching at the bottom of the stroke and compensating by going toes-down, that can be another sign the saddle is too high.

In a recent development, rocking hips can also happen with a saddle that’s too low. So can a toes-down pedaling style. Tight hamstrings, limited mobility, weak core stability, and other fit problems can all muddy the picture. Back-of-knee pain can come from saddle height, but it can also come from saddle fore-aft, cleat setup, or a combination of things.

That doesn’t make the signs worthless. It just means you should think in patterns, not absolutes.

If you have knee pain plus hip rocking plus pressure and instability in the saddle, now the case gets stronger.

Todd Carver, Specialized’s human performance manager, shared a simple check that can help flag a saddle that may be too high.

If the distance from heel to pedal is more than about one centimeter, your saddle could be too high.

The result is a prompt to look closer, not a green light to make significant changes without further investigation.

Recent findings suggest that don’t make a giant change. That’s how you turn one problem into several problems.

Start small. Lower the saddle a few millimeters at a time, then ride it long enough to notice whether the change actually helps. One short spin around the block is not enough. You want enough ride time to see whether the pain eases, whether your pedaling feels smoother, and whether you stop shifting around on the saddle.

If you’re dealing with persistent pain, don’t keep self-diagnosing forever.

A good fit pro can sort out whether saddle height is the actual problem or just the most obvious symptom.

Riders fixate on saddle height because it feels fundamental. And it is. But it’s also just one part of a system.

A high saddle can absolutely cause trouble. So can cleat position. So can saddle setback. So can crank length. So can your mobility. The goal is not to chase some magic formula you found online. It’s to get to a position that lets you pedal smoothly, make power comfortably, and finish rides feeling worked, not damaged.

That’s why the best takeaway is a modest one: use the common signs, do a quick check, make small changes, and listen to what your body tells you.

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Next up on his to-do list: a multi day bikepacking trip, and an e-bike race.

How to Watch the 2026 NCAA Cross Country Championships

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

The collegiate fall racing calendar isn't quite finished, with the 2026 NCAA Cross Country National Championships bringing together teams and individual athletes looking to end their seasons with a title.

Division I gets underway Saturday, November 21, in Terre Haute, Indiana, where 32 men's teams and 32 women's teams will compete. Alongside them will be 38 individual qualifiers whose schools didn't make the team field.

If you've been keeping a close eye on college cross country this season, there's plenty to be excited about this weekend. Oklahoma State returns as the defending men's team champion and winners of two of the past three titles, while NC State's women will look to add another trophy to a particularly successful stretch of their own, having collected four championships since 2021.

In a recent development, fortunately, you don't have to make the trip to Indiana to catch the action. Here's when everything starts, where the races are being held, and how to watch from home.

The Division I and Division III championships will both take place on Saturday, November 21, although the two competitions will be held in different states.

Division II runners will have to wait a little longer, with their national championship scheduled for Friday, December 4.

According to the NCAA's championship schedule, here's where each division will compete:.

In a recent development, for Division I, ESPNU and the ESPN app will carry the national championships live on Saturday, November 21, with coverage beginning at 10 a.m. ET.

The women's 6K starts at 10:20 a.m., followed by the men's 10K at 11:10 a.m., and the trophy presentation scheduled for around noon.

Fans following Divisions II and III can watch their respective competitions through the NCAA.com's live streaming schedule.

Oklahoma State has been tough to beat in recent years, finishing near the top of the men’s standings more often than not. The Cowboys have claimed two of the last five national titles, winning the national title in 2025, with 57 points, 25 points ahead of runner-up New Mexico.

In a recent development, NC State’s women have enjoyed a similarly strong run, having won three straight titles from 2021 to 2023, before BYU took the 2024 championship. NC State reclaimed the top spot last year, with 114 points.

Division I's national field includes 32 teams per gender, with 18 earning automatic spots through the nine regional championships and another 14 receiving bids through an at-large selection process.

There are also 38 individual qualifiers in each race, representing schools that didn't advance as teams, so the competition for the individual titles extends well beyond the athletes wearing jerseys from the leading programs. With both individual and team titles on the line, there's plenty to follow once the starting gun goes off.

U.S. Women Could Be Upgraded to World Half Marathon Gold After Kenyan Runner’s EPO Ban

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (527 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Emma Grace Hurley, Weini Kelati, and Jess McClain already had plenty to celebrate after earning the United States its first women's team medal at September's World Road Running Championships in Copenhagen.
  • According to recent reports, on Thursday, November 19, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) declared that Kenya's Veronica Loleo had received a three-year doping ban after testing positive for erythropoietin (EPO), a prohibited substance.
  • The Kenyan women originally led with a combined 3:17:33, ahead of the Americans' 3:19:51.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Emma Grace Hurley, Weini Kelati, and Jess McClain already had plenty to celebrate after earning the United States its first women's team medal at September's World Road Running Championships in Copenhagen. But nearly two months after finishing with silver, the American trio could soon have gold added to their résumés.

According to recent reports, on Thursday, November 19, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) declared that Kenya's Veronica Loleo had received a three-year doping ban after testing positive for erythropoietin (EPO), a prohibited substance. The decision officially disqualifies her second-place finish at the September 20 event, where her silver medal helped Kenya secure the women's team title. But with Loleo's result now thrown out, Kenya's team score has to be recalculated. Countries are ranked by the combined finishing times of their three fastest athletes, and Loleo’s removal means Kenya must now count Lilian Kasait Rengeruk, who finished 34th in 1:10:36, potentially lifting the U.S. to first place in the team standings.

The Kenyan women originally led with a combined 3:17:33, ahead of the Americans' 3:19:51. But removing Loleo's 1:06:05 pushes Kenya's total to 3:22:04, leaving the U.S. in first place by two minutes and 13 seconds. Kenya would drop to second and Ethiopia would remain third, although World Athletics has yet to officially confirm the updated results.

According to recent reports, hurley recently acknowledged the uncertainty in a comment on Citius Mag's Instagram, noting that nobody can know exactly how the race would've unfolded without Loleo. Still, she admitted, "it would've been so cool to celebrate gold 🥹.".

Recent findings suggest that loleo's sample was collected during an out-of-competition test on September 6 ahead of the championships, two weeks prior to the competition. She initially told investigators she couldn't explain the positive result, mentioning an injection she'd received for an injury, but later admitted to the violation on October 30, which earned her a one-year reduction from the standard four-year suspension.

According to recent reports, loleo wasn't the only major Kenyan distance runner to receive a final decision Thursday. Peres Jepchirchir, the reigning world marathon champion and 2021 Olympic gold medalist, was also handed a three-year ban following an EPO finding.

“The Kenyan authorities have made a lot of progress in the fight against doping in the last five years, but these cases highlight that there is still a long way to go,” AIU chief executive Brett Clothier said in a statement.

“The Kenyan government is aware of the current situation and has committed to further strengthen the Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya and take action to address the criminal networks that facilitate doping within the country.”.

According to recent reports, jepchirchir, who had been provisionally suspended in October, has accepted the disqualification of her results dating back to July 17, including her August victory at the Sydney Marathon. Fellow Kenyan Irine Cheptai is expected to inherit that title.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Sources indicate that there are plenty of reasons to start riding inside. Questionable weather, overly packed schedules, and less daylight can cause outdoor riders to head inside for some indoor saddle time. It’s also possible you’re someone who doesn’t ride outside and you just want a good low-impact workout in the comfort of your own home—without breaking the bank.

Recently we did extensive testing in the office on different exercise bikes. I found that some people who don’t ride bikes outside may actually prefer some of the less expensive exercise bike options. Some of the higher-end exercise bikes we tested feel like a real bike outside—and pair with specific apps like Zwift for when you want to get some group rides or racing in. If you aren’t used to a bike outside, then getting comfortable in that position can be a hard transition. More narrow saddles, a more aggressive position, and controls that simulate the shifters on a bike may not be what you want. Largely, these more inexpensive exercise bikes have more upright positions, wider and more padded saddles, and controls that would resemble the exercise bike you might see on the floor of a fitness center.

It has been revealed that keep in mind that inexpensive is relative—the bikes we have on this list range from about $200 up to $700. If you’re looking to boost your mood, stay consistent, or supplement your training with an affordable indoor cycling bike, these cheap exercise bikes deliver the best mix of value, performance, and reliability.

If you're further along in your indoor training journey and none of the bikes on this list feel like the right fit, take a look at our reviews of the Peloton, Zwift Ride V2, and other premium models.

This budget-priced, belt-driven bike operates a 35-pound flywheel that provides a smooth and quiet ride. The resistance is adjustable via a knob regardless of pedaling speed. It also has an emergency brake that stops the flywheel immediately, if necessary. According to Yosuda, the seat height adjusts to fit riders with inseams from 25 to 35 inches, and allows riders to adjust the handlebar height as well as the fore-aft alignment of the padded saddle.

Using the single-button monitor, you can scroll through your time, speed, distance, and calories burned as you exercise. Just below the monitor is a platform for a phone or tablet. The heavy-duty steel frame is designed to provide stability and durability, but it's easy to move if you tip it up onto the small wheels on the front edge.

Besides being designed to look like an entry-level Peloton, the Yesoul S3’s biggest selling point is its Bluetooth connectivity, which pairs with the Yesoul Sports App (on both iOS and Android) and works with Zwift and other interactive training apps. All your workout data, including distance, time, calories burned, speed, heart rate, odometer, and cadence, is tracked and easy to access.

Recent findings suggest that the bike has a quiet belt drive and magnetic resistance, with 100 levels that are easy to adjust with a knob. With a height- and distance-adjustable seat and handlebar, the S3 is built to fit riders from 4-feet-9-inches to 6-feet-2-inches—though riders at the higher end of that range and those with disproportionately longer legs might find the riding position to feel a bit “off.” The bike is easy to move on two small transport wheels, and it comes in both white and black models for a sleek, Peloton-like aesthetic.

This is a fantastic price for a budget bike that delivers a Peloton-like experience. It has the same sleek silhouette, with a saddle that adjusts both up/down and fore/aft, plus an adjustable handlebar height—just like the real thing. The belt-drive system is another big plus, keeping noise to a minimum so the only sounds you hear are your own effort (and hopefully some music to cover it up).

To keep costs down, this bike skips the large built-in display, instead offering a tablet holder and Bluetooth connectivity. That means you can ride with any third-party app you prefer—including Peloton classes—using your own device. At this price, it’s a fair trade-off. But if you want a built-in screen, Merach offers a similar model with that feature for about $450 more.

Sources indicate that merach’s newest bike, the A26 Aura, is one of the best Peloton competitors I’ve seen. It follows the familiar design cues of premium exercise bikes — a sturdy frame, heavy flywheel, and whisper-quiet belt-drive system. The seat adjusts up and down as well as fore and aft, and the handlebar also moves vertically for a comfortable fit.

At its current sale price, the Merach A26 Aura makes a compelling case as one of the best values on this list.

The Echelon Connect Sport 2 delivers a Peloton-like experience at a more affordable price. It connects via Bluetooth to the Echelon Fit app, allowing you to track speed, distance, and calories. If you’re taking a live class, you can also view your ranking on the leaderboard. The app offers over 40 live classes daily and a library of more than 15,000 on-demand sessions. While the bike doesn’t have a built-in screen, its device holder accommodates tablets up to 8 inches wide.

Industry observers note that that mentioned, you don’t need the connected features to get a great workout. At its core, this is a solid, well-built exercise bike with a heavy flywheel and 32 resistance levels, manually adjusted with a knob behind the handlebar. The bike features a “one size fits most” design, with adjustable saddle and handlebar positions to suit most adults. However, some shorter riders have reported difficulty positioning the saddle close enough to the handlebars for a comfortable fit.

Sources indicate that with Bluetooth and USB connectivity to the Schwinn ConnectTM, Zwift, and MyFitnessPal apps, this stationary bike is a great option for interactive workouts—particularly if you want to work through pre-programmed sessions and track your progress over time. The bike has the standard DualTrack console shared by similar-level Schwinn and Nautilus products, which has two sharp, backlit LCD screens loaded with 29 workouts.

It has been revealed that unlike many of the bikes we've selected that adjust gradually in difficulty at the turn of a knob, this model has 25 preset levels of magnetic resistance, which provides a nice range in difficulty. The seat and handlebar adjust by height and angle to fit customers from 4-feet-6-inches to 6-feet-6-inches; however, as always, those at the far ends of the range might have more difficulty getting a comfortable fit. Ultimately, the bike is a solid package for the price—especially if you can catch one on sale for around $400.

Looking for a cheap home exercise bike that will neither take over your space nor break the bank? When not in use, this compact device folds down to half its size and can be easily rolled into a closet or tucked under a bed.

It has been revealed that while it may have a minimalist design, it still has the basic functionality needed for a workout. It touts 12 levels of magnetic resistance, adjusted via a knob below the handlebar, that allows you to adjust the intensity as needed. The built-in LCD screen, although very basic, keeps track of key workout stats, including distance, time, speed, calories burned, and heart rate.

Sources indicate that consumers love how quiet this bike is, making it perfect for multitasking or watching TV while riding. Though it may not provide the high resistance some hardcore riders seek, many praise it as a “sturdy, well-built machine” with a “comfortable seat and great height adjustability.”.

Sources indicate that just like with a regular bicycle, if you want the best experience on your indoor bike, it’s important to get the proper fit. Josh Taylor, a global brand ambassador for the online fitness site Spinning, recommends finding an indoor cycling bike that puts you in the same position as the bike you’re accustomed to riding outside.

For example, if your daily rider is a road bike, look for an indoor cycling bike with a handlebar option that incorporates a traditional bullhorn bar and mimics the hand-position options of drops and brake hoods. However, if you’re already used to taking studio classes, an indoor cycling bike with just the traditional bullhorn-style bar will work great, notes Ben Sharp, three-time Order of Ikkos medal recipient and founder of Sharp Coaching.

It has been revealed that if you don’t ride at all outside or in a spin class yet, then it will take a bit more playing around with the exercise bike to figure out sizing and position. Start with getting saddle height set up correctly, then if you can adjust reach to the handlebars that’s step two. For the reach shoot to have a slight bend in the elbows and remember to keep your shoulders relaxed and away from your ears. Matt Phillips, Senior Test Editor at Bicycling, recently published a story on dialing in saddle height. What applies to saddle height on an outdoor bike largely applies to exercise bikes as well. “A common starting point is a height that provides around 30 degrees of knee bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke (6 o’clock position). But that is a starting point only, not gospel,” says Phillips.

Join Bicycling All Access for more in-depth gear reviews.

When you’re riding an outdoor bike, you’re mostly working against inertia as you pedal. In order to recreate that sensation and effort on a stationary bike, manufacturers have to simulate that resistance in some way. Most choose to use a fan or a flywheel (a weighted disc that spins as you pedal).

Sources indicate that flywheels work by storing inertia as they spin, and smoothing out the pedal stroke to eliminate that choppy up and down motion you’d otherwise experience. For most budget spin bikes, a heavier flywheel means a smoother ride, though some bikes opt for a light (8-pound) flywheel that maintains its inertia by spinning four times as fast instead.

According to recent reports, since the pedals on spin bikes are fixed to the flywheel (no coasting), the smooth-moving mechanism helps keep your pedaling consistent. These bikes will usually have a knob or lever that allows you to adjust the resistance, making it harder or easier to pedal, independent of your cadence (how fast you’re spinning the pedals). If you’re used to riding a bike outside, then think about it like riding a fixed-gear bike or fixie.

Fan-operated resistance bikes are a bit simpler: As you pedal, the fan blades push against the air around the machine. Your cadence is directly related to the amount of effort required to push the pedals, meaning these bikes don’t allow you to spin at a fast cadence with low resistance, which can be nice for warming up or cooling down.

This Mileage Target Can Help You Determine Whether You Built a Strong Enough Base to Start Race Training

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

  • Sources indicate that building a sufficient aerobic base helps you avoid the aches and pains that come with ramping up mileage too quickly, especially if you’ve been running sporadically or took some time off.
  • It has been revealed that the hard part of this foundational phase?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that base training involves spending a few weeks running at an easy pace and slowly increasing your mileage over time. It’s a crucial first step in any running journey, designed to help you ease into race-specific training.

Sources indicate that building a sufficient aerobic base helps you avoid the aches and pains that come with ramping up mileage too quickly, especially if you’ve been running sporadically or took some time off. It also makes running feel more doable, as it bridges the gap between your current routine and your goal training strategy.

It has been revealed that the hard part of this foundational phase? Figuring out if you’re ready to tackle the first few weeks of a blueprint and start race-specific workouts. Thankfully, coaches offer a helpful benchmark to hit, plus they explain how to smoothly transition your base routine to race training, without shocking your system.

In a recent development, building a strong base before racing any distance helps prevent injuries and improves long-term performance, including improved aerobic capacity, endurance, faster recovery, mental conditioning, and weight and stress management, Jill Becker, a personal trainer and run coach at Life Time in Westminster, CO, previously told Runner’s World. That’s why the phase is necessary for all runners, whether you’re upcoming to the sport or have a Boston qualifying time on the list of goals.

“Even a 5K race relies heavily on aerobic systems for energy production—so the better the aerobic base you have, the faster you can race,” Laura Norris, owner and coach at Laura Norris Running in Boulder, CO, previously told Runner’s World.

According to recent reports, additionally, Norris notes doing these easy miles weeks before your goal training block allows your body to adapt to the mileage first, so you can then add in speedwork leading up to race day with lower risk of injury and burnout. Taking this approach helps you avoid increasing volume and intensity at the same time, which can often lead to overtraining.

Finally, tackling a base phase means you’ll feel more confident heading into, say, a four-miler with faster-paced efforts (like tempo or race pace miles), as you’ll have already run four miles at an easy pace consistently for several weeks.

Building a strong base requires covering a certain number of miles consistently over the course of several weeks. Beginners should aim to spend at least 10 weeks on this training block, while intermediate runners can follow a six-week proposal, and more advanced runners typically need about four weeks to set that aerobic foundation, Becker states.

According to recent reports, if you’ve already picked out your training plan, Norris recommends working up to at least 80 percent of the weekly mileage prescribed in the first week of that plan. For example, our 20-week beginner marathon plan prescribes 12 miles in the first week. That means you’ll want to work up to about 10 miles per week before diving into the plan. If you’re looking to break two hours in the half marathon, which requires running at least 18 miles in the first week of the Runner’s World plan, then you’ll want to work up to about 15 miles.

If you haven’t identified your training plan yet, Becker recommends adding at least 10 miles to your current weekly volume. (If you’re presently running 10 miles a week, work up to 20.).

Look for a blueprint that builds up to that mileage goal slowly, following the 10 percent rule, which means increasing your mileage by no more than 10 percent each week.

It has been revealed that keep in mind, base training is about setting the foundation for your next training block, and a part of that process should include recovery time. This means making time for rest days and down weeks (in which you reduce your volume to allow for recovery and better performance), as well as staying on top of your nutrition, sleep habits, and cross-training.

Monique LeBrun is a health and fitness editor who is based in Easton, Pennsylvania. She covers a wide range of health and wellness topics, with a primary focus on running performance and nutrition. Monique is passionate about creating content that empowers runners to become the best versions of themselves. Our Editors Rode Dozens of E-Bikes. These 12 Are Worth Buying for Commuting, Trails, Cargo, and Tight Budgets

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that you wouldn’t think late autumn is the best time to buy an electric bike; after all, the daylight hours are short, and the weather is getting cold in many regions.
  • In a recent development, I’m a lifelong cyclist, former product director for bike companies, and was a mechanic at busy shops in New York City.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Sources indicate that you wouldn’t think late autumn is the best time to buy an electric bike; after all, the daylight hours are short, and the weather is getting cold in many regions. However, whether you’re hunting for deals or seeking out the latest tech, now is the time to buy. With holiday discounts and fresh e-bikes rolling out to dealers and online retailers, plenty of great commuter, cargo, and e-MTB options are out there—at great prices.

In a recent development, I’m a lifelong cyclist, former product director for bike companies, and was a mechanic at busy shops in New York City. Plus, I commute daily on an e-bike and ride test dozens of electric bikes each year. Last summer, I even went almost entirely car-free thanks to an electric cargo bike.

Sources indicate that whether you’re choosing your first e-bike, upgrading to a newer model, or adding another electric model to your garage, dozens of great options are available—and our editors and staff have tested many of them. No matter your age, cycling ability, or budget, brands offer electric bikes that meet needs.

According to recent reports, tip for E-Bike Buyers: Don’t overpay for an electric bike, but spend what you can comfortably afford. If an e-bike is fun to ride, you’ll use it more often. It’s more cost-effective to buy an e-bike equipped the way you want it upfront than to upgrade it later. Also, remember: you cannot change an electric bike’s motor system if you decide you want more power.

Recent findings suggest that the Aventon Level is our benchmark electric bike. It’s a great e-bike for commuting, running errands, or leisure riding. Over several years, the Level platform has proven to be reliable and low-maintenance. Plus, its price doesn’t break the bank.

According to recent reports, aventon split the 4th-generation Level into two models. The REC features a 750W hub motor with 80 Nm of torque. Aventon also added regenerative braking, increasing the bike’s range up to 75 miles. The pricier ADV edition features a mid-drive motor; it bumps up the torque to 100 Nm and range to 110 miles. Both versions come standard with fenders, a rear rack, lights, and suspension.

It has been revealed that another feature users will find quite useful is the Level’s connected features. The Level 4’s ACU (Aventon Control Unit) adds several smart features to the already well-equipped platform. The wheel lock and motion sensor alarm are passive theft deterrents when you stop for a mid-ride coffee or run into the post office. A 4G chip in the ACU enables GPS tracking in Aventon’s mobile app, so you can locate your bike if you forget where you locked it. 4G connectivity also allows you to set geofence restrictions on the bike for teens or housemates.

BUY LEVEL 4 STEP-THROUGH BUY LEVEL 4 ADV.

Sources indicate that the relatively affordable seven-speed model Soltera 2.5 from Aventon delivers simplicity and style that is tough to beat. This makes it an excellent choice for getting around town or quick commutes. It’s even better than the original version, thanks to hydraulic disc brakes. A push of the throttle gets you started; then, the brushless hub motor gently assists your pedaling.

In a recent development, along with disc brakes, the Soltera features integrated lights and turn signals, and the battery is hidden in the bike’s frame (rather than the bolt-on batteries found on many similarly-priced e-bikes). Best for smoother roads and bike paths, the Soltera delivers the essential features a city rider needs in a strikingly light 46-pound package.

Aventon also offers a singlespeed, Soltera 3 ADV with a Gates belt-drive system.

When buying a low-priced e-bike, a simple, low-cost, easy-to-repair, and reliable model usually beats out complicated designs. Lectric’s XP Lite2 is about as basic as it gets. It has a low-maintenance singlespeed drivetrain, a 300-watt hub motor, and a 375Wh battery. With its compact size, 20x2.5-inch tires, and twist-grip throttle, the XP Lite is perfect for zipping through traffic, commuting to the office, or heading to the gym or bar after work.

The XP Lite2 features only one gear and a 300W motor, so it’s not ideal for very hilly terrain. But with the throttle, you can get over small rises and bridges. Lectric also equips the bike with hydraulic disc brakes and front and rear lights. The XP Lite2 is also great for RVers and campgrounds, since it’s lightweight (about 48 pounds) and folds down to 36x16x27-inch dimensions.

Many “step-through” e-bikes don’t actually have a low step design. This makes it challenging for some riders to mount or dismount. However, the CTY e2.1, by REI’s Co-op house brand, has a fully step-through front triangle. The CTY is a great choice for older riders, those with reduced mobility, or others who seek an easy-to-ride e-bike.

According to recent reports, REI equips the CTY e2.1 with a 250-watt hub-drive motor that provides smooth pedal-assistance up to 20 mph. It also features a suspension fork to smooth out bumps and potholes, an adjustable stem for a comfortable riding position, and hydraulic disc brakes for better stopping. For less than the cost of some e-bikes online, you can get a quality electric bike backed up by REI warranty and service.

Sources indicate that the Current ADV is the priciest bike in this story, but for a good reason. Some electric bikes look a lot like mountain bikes, but that doesn’t mean they are built for real off-road use. Aventon’s latest Current is the brand’s first full suspension E-MTB, and it is trail-ready right out of the box. Trevor Raab, Bicycling’s Senior Photographer and Test Team member, mentioned, “The bike’s intuitive ride feel will please experienced mountain bikers and also benefit first-time mountain bikers.”.

Sources indicate that the Current ADV features an aluminum frame with 140mm rear wheel travel and a great-feeling motor with 750 peak Watts and 110 Nm of torque. (It also has a Boost mode that bumps power to 850W and 120 Nm of torque.) Rounding out the ADV are high-end components like a RockShox Psylo Gold fork, SRAM DB8 brakes, SRAM Eagle 70 Mechanical transmission, and a tubeless wheelset with Maxxis Minion EXO tires.

In his full review of the bike, “Aventon Goes Full Performance: The Current Electric Mountain Bike Is Surprisingly Dialed,” Raab particularly likes the Current’s easy-to-use interface. It’s loaded with ride data as well as the ability to tune the motor settings. If you don’t need rear suspension, check out Aventon’s updated Ramblas ADV hardtail E-MTB.

READ AVENTON CURRENT REVIEWMORE GREAT E-MTBs.

Getting into E-MTB trail riding on a budget is tough. Low-priced electric mountain bikes often aren’t built strong enough for off-road riding (or weigh half a rider’s weight), and trail-capable models typically cost more than $4,000. That’s what makes the TrailRush a standout bike—for less than $2,000, you get a trail-ready hardtail you can take on singletrack and have some fun.

Ride1Up equips the 29-inch-wheeled TrailRush with a Brose mid-drive motor. With 90 Nm of torque, it isn’t as powerful as many latest, higher-priced E-MTB motors, but it gets the job done. The TrailRush also comes stock with a dropper seatpost, four-piston disc brakes, and tubeless-compatible rims with Maxxis Minion tires.

Recent findings suggest that of course, to hit this great price, Ride1Up made some equipment sacrifices. The 504Wh battery isn’t as large as some peers (like the Aventon Ramblas), so you get less ride time between charges. Additionally, the 11-36T cassette and 38T chainring limit your ability to climb steep hills.

Compared to earlier iterations of the Aventure, the third-generation model has a smoother ride and feels more like a premium bike (without the high price tag). Aventon’s fresh torque sensor allows more control over the acceleration of Aventure’s 750W rear hub motor. Lighter-weight testers found earlier models had too much torque, but this Aventure remedied that fault. Additional features include a new head-unit interface, integrated turn signals, a front light, a rear rack, and fenders.

The Aventure 3 is an excellent fat-tire e-bike for commuters—especially on snowy days and gravel paths. Off-roading, it excels on doubletrack trails and cinder paths, but with this burly bike’s weight and components, it has limited functionality on singletrack and more aggressive mountain trails.

Aventon also offers the Aventure M, a mid-drive version of the Aventure. It keeps the same major, burly character but adds a more premium feel, a smoother, more powerful motor, and an upgraded drivetrain—along with a higher price. Those refinements cost about $1,000 more than the Aventure 3.

Buying an e-bike on Amazon can be risky, especially if you don’t know much about bikes or have limited mechanical experience. However, sometimes you can find a good deal on a decent bike. At $500, the Heybike Cityscape isn’t the pinnacle of e-bike technology, but it lets you get out and enjoy some rides without breaking the bank.

It has been revealed that I combed through dozens of Amazon listings comparing low-priced electric bikes, and this Heybike stood out for its combination of price and features. Then, I saw someone on the local bike path with one and asked them about the bike. The rider liked it and mentioned it has been trouble-free (they noted a local bike shop assembled it for them). Heybike’s U.S. support line is available for warranty service or product questions.

Sources indicate that don’t want to purchase from Amazon? Use this exclusive Bicycling discount link for $100 (applied at checkout) off the Cityscape 2.0, plus free shipping.

Tern’s cargo bikes are the gold standard for practical features, durability, and ride quality. This reputation makes the brand’s GSD (longtail) and HSD (short-tail) cargo models top picks for bike commuters, families, and riders looking to cut their dependence on automobiles.

According to recent reports, the latest third-generation HSD improves on its predecessor’s legacy. The HSD (short for “Haul Stuff Daily”) is a shrunken-down version of Tern’s GSD3 model released last year. The HSD3’s frame has a 419-pound carrying capacity (combined bike, rider, and cargo), added stiffness, and improved stability at speed compared to its predecessor. The P10e Sport configuration features the peppier Bosch Performance Line Sport motor and an electronic-shifting ten-speed TRP E.A.S.I. A10 drivetrain. The Sport motor’s 28mph assistance was a welcome upgrade for commuting and running errands alongside car traffic on local suburban streets. The 90 Nm of torque (15 Nm more than the standard Performance Line motor) also provides quicker acceleration from a dead stop and a little more oomph when loaded down with cargo or climbing hills.

In a recent development, while it’s the second-most affordable HSD3 model in Tern’s U.S. selection, the P10e Sport is certainly not a budget-priced e-bike. But for the extra cost over similar-sized cargo bikes, you get a proven and well-thought-out bicycle. The HSD’s features and design elements feel purposeful. A great example of this is the bike’s stowability: The HSD3 can be tilted and stored vertically, balanced on its rear rack. It also moves easily on its rear wheel when you need to park or store it. The handlebar and stem also fold down, making the HSD3 much easier to transport by car or SUV than almost any other e-bike.

It has been revealed that many riders are attracted to the XPedition’s very appealing price. Currently priced at $1,399 for the single-battery model, it boasts an impressive 60-mile range and a top speed of 28 mph. (The dual-battery model for $1,799 doubles the range to 120 miles.) This makes the XPedition one of the most affordable electric cargo bikes around and a good option for riders seeking an excellent deal on an e-cargo bike.

In a recent development, “The XPedition’s capability surprised me”, stated Test Editor Dan Chabanov. “Combined with the Lectric XL panniers ($150) and the Essentials package ($120), I comfortably carried several days of groceries for a family of three or one adult passenger.”.

However, to reach a price like this, concessions have to be made somewhere. This results in a somewhat cheap feeling to the bike. Most of the XPedition’s parts are bottom-tier—with the notable exception of the brakes. The pedal-assist motor is powerful off the line, but at times, it feels erratic. The XPedition is adequate if you live in a very flat area or don’t need to carry kids or an adult passenger. Despite these faults, if you’re on a budget and looking to ditch the car for errands and trips around town, the XPedition is the cheapest e-cargo bike we recommend buying.

Plenty of commuter e-bikes cost far less than Specialized’s Turbo Vado SL 2, and they can probably do most of these things. So why spend twice as much as many popular options? I dive into the details in my story, “Stop Wasting Money on Cheap E-Bikes. Here’s Why Spending More Pays Off for Commuters.”.

The TL;DR: The Turbo Vado SL 2’s excellent ride geometry, silky-smooth motor, low weight, and premium components make riding fun. Together, these features make you want to ride the Vado every day and use it for more than simply getting to work. And thanks to Specialized’s extensive dealer network, you have somewhere to turn when it needs service.

Industry observers note that “Lightweight e-bike” might sound like an oxymoron to some, but a sub-40-pound weight is impressive when many electric bikes exceed 60 or 80 pounds. And often, e-bikes this light are pricey. Yet, the Velotric Tempo is only $1,499 and boasts a 39 lb. (claimed) weight.

Velotric achieves this weight reduction by ditching the bulky suspension fork (suspension forks on lower-priced bikes often don’t work all that well, to be frank), swapping heavy tires for 700x42c gravel tires, and using a smaller battery. Riders who need to carry the bike up any stairs or load it onto a bike rack will appreciate the reduced weight. However, heavier riders may want to test ride the Tempo before purchase, as lower-powered motors can bog down and reduce battery range for bigger-bodied people.

Sources indicate that bicycles are my life, and I’m a dedicated e-bike user and enthusiast. I’ve also worked in cycling for over 25 years. For almost six years, I’ve ridden and tested electric bikes as Bicycling’s Deputy Editor—and I use e-bikes for my daily commute. Before joining the staff, I led product development for top bicycle brands.

According to recent reports, our editors test dozens of electric bikes across every cycling category, and we continually receive fresh models to evaluate. Our riding involves much more than taking bikes on short spins; we use electric bikes in our daily lives. Commuting, school drop-offs, grocery runs, and daily transportation are only a few of the things we regularly do with e-bikes. We also hit the trails on E-MTB models to test their performance in real-world mountain biking conditions, not simply riding them around town.

Industry observers note that in addition to ride-testing, our editors regularly talk to cyclists of all ages and abilities about their riding needs. This helps us craft our list of Best Electric Bikes: e-bikes that will meet your needs on the street, trails, and around the neighborhood. Two of the e-bikes in this story even made the final cut for our 2026 Bike Awards.

Electric bike prices range from entry-level models for less than $500 to premium machines costing almost as much as a good used car. However, our years of testing have proven that many of the best and most practical models live squarely in the middle.

We find that many standout e-bikes are priced between $1,500 and $3,000. These models strike a good balance between reliability and practicality, without requiring you to overspend on features or technology you don’t need. Electric bikes costing less than $1,000 often take shortcuts to achieve this, either by using lower-quality parts or offering limited service after the bike is purchased.

Of course, you can also spend much more on electric bikes. Premium e-bikes typically offer improved motor performance, higher-quality components, lower weight, or more tech features. However, for most general riding purposes, these bikes are overkill—but they‘re certainly fun!

Sources indicate that → Consider how much cargo you’ll need to carry if your riding involves commuting or running errands. Look for a bike with appropriate racks, mount points, and other accessories.

→ For singletrack and trail riding, look for mountain bikes with knobby tires, adjustable suspension, high-quality frames, and low weight.

It has been revealed that → Pay attention to weight. While fat tire e-bikes and cargo bikes offer versatility, many weigh over 90 pounds. If you’ll need to carry your bike up any stairs or lift it onto a bike rack, a lighter option will be a better fit.

In a recent development, → Bike storage is another consideration. While most e-bikes don’t require excessive space compared to their non-pedal-assisted counterparts, ensure you have access to a power outlet where you plan to store it for easy charging.

It has been revealed that several e-bike brands, Aventon, Ride1Up, and Lectric, performed well in our ride testing and evaluations. These bikes might require some minor assembly at home, such as installing pedals, a seat, and tightening handlebars. We considered how easy bikes were to assemble in our recommendations. Many bike shops will not assemble or otherwise work on e-bikes they do not sell due to liability issues. The direct-to-consumer brands we recommend have dealers nationwide ready to support you.

Established bike companies, such as Specialized and Trek, manufacture e-bikes and have hundreds of dealers across North America. Additionally, REI sells its house-brand Co-op electric bikes (and models from Cannondale and Tern) in its stores.

Sources indicate that there are three electric-assist classes available in the United States, and the use of each class of bike can vary by state, city, and area you are riding. Be sure to check local regulations before buying and before riding your bike.

Class 1: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment.

Class 2: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle comes standard equipment.

Class 3: 28 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment.

What this means: Class 1 motors kick in only when you pedal and stop helping you at 20 mph. Class 2 also offers pedal assist up to 20 mph, but these bikes can also have a throttle-powered mode that allows users to engage the motor without pedaling. Class 3 is pedal-assist like Class 1, but helps you until you reach 28 mph.

Other countries classify electric bikes differently, and many do not allow e-bikes to assist riders beyond 20 miles per hour.

Electric bikes generally feature one of two types of motors: mid-drive motors, which are contained in the frame at the bottom of the bike between the pedals; and rear hub motors, which are built into the rear wheel.

In a recent development, bikes with rear hub motors are generally less expensive but are also less powerful. Mid-drive e-bikes tend to be more expensive, but are typically more reliable and higher performance. Because the extra weight on a mid-drive motor is centered in the bike and lower to the ground, these bikes are generally easier to handle than bikes with hub motors.

According to recent reports, measured in Newton meters (or Nm), torque is a rotational measurement of force—and the number to pay attention to when you want an idea of an e-bike motor’s output. More torque means more power off the line and more boost to your pedaling.

According to recent reports, the heavier the bike, the more torque it needs. Lighter road bikes typically have 30 to 40 Nm of torque, and trail and cargo models (generally) have at least 80 Nm. Most commuter bikes fall somewhere in between.

The size of an e-bike’s battery is measured in watt-hours (or Wh). This measurement represents the energy stored in the battery and how many watts it can deliver each hour. The higher the number, the longer the range, but the faster you go, the faster you drain the battery.

So, if a 504Wh battery paired with a 500W motor gives you one hour of ride time at the highest assist, riding at about half that power will double your range.

In a recent development, many e-bike brands seamlessly integrate batteries to make the bike look sleeker (and more like a traditional non-assist bike). Most batteries lock to the bike and come with a key that lets you unlock and remove it, which serves multiple purposes: You can remove the battery and charge it off the bike, plus a locked battery deters (and hopefully prevents) a thief from stealing it. An e-bike with the battery removed is safer for hauling on a bike rack and lighter for carrying up steps.

Recent findings suggest that since e-bikes can maintain higher speeds for longer than standard bikes, you want extra control when riding. Wider tires provide better traction and the freedom to leave the pavement with little penalty, and a suspension fork will help tame some of the rougher roads you might explore. Good disc brakes are a must, too, for slowing a heavy bike at high speed. This is not a place to skimp.

It has been revealed that some e-bikes have an integrated lighting system that turns on when you power up the bike. While this is a great feature, it’s not a deal-breaker if your bike doesn’t come equipped this way. It’s just as easy to attach your own since so many great bike lights are available.

According to recent reports, E-bikes need regular maintenance and repair to stay in good working condition. Because they’re heavier and go faster than non-assist bicycles, e-bikes often require more regular service on parts like brakes, tires, and drivetrain components. We recommend having a good relationship with a local bike shop experienced in e-bike repair to keep your equipment running smoothly.

Industry observers note that E-bikes use electronics for their motors, batteries, and displays. These parts are often proprietary to bike brands or even specific e-bike models, making replacement more difficult than parts on non-electric bicycles. Make sure to use the correct electronic replacement parts to avoid damaging your e-bike (or it catching fire).

Established brands usually (but not always) have a good supply of these parts for replacement, even for years after a bike goes out of production. Bosch and Shimano are two e-bike motor manufacturers with some of the most compatibility between bikes and stock parts for previous generations of systems.

According to recent reports, look for e-bikes from brands that offer at least a one-year warranty on electronic components (many brands’ warranties are longer) and make items like replacement batteries for your bike. These parts are usually not cheap (sometimes up to half the cost of a new bike), but it’s the difference between having an e-bike that can be repaired or becomes a bicycle-shaped paperweight if something goes wrong.

Following a dramatic increase in fires caused by the lithium-ion batteries used in electric bikes, there is a push from local officials, regulatory agencies, and advocacy groups across the U.S. for improved safety certification of e-bikes, batteries, and motor units. In September 2023, a Upcoming York City law took effect requiring that any e-bike sold in the city “has been certified by an accredited testing laboratory for compliance with Underwriters Laboratories (UL) standard 2849”.

It has been revealed that however, just because something is marketed as UL 2849 compliant, tested to UL 2849, or even “certified to UL 2849” does not mean it is UL Safety Certified. Ibrahim Jilani, UL’s Global Director of Consumer Technology, notes: “Certification is always earned by a manufacturer and not a given when they undergo a product submittal. The UL Mark, or any authorized certification mark, can only be issued upon successful demonstration of meeting the requirements of the safety standard.” You can find UL’s updated list of products certified to UL 2849 here. You can cross-reference OSHA’s Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratories for a deep dive into the topic.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Fresh England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Assault Bike ProX is one of the best cardio machines presently offered, as it provides a full-body, low-impact workout that can still be high-intensity.
  • It has been revealed that here at Breaking Muscle, our experts include athletes, strength and conditioning coaches, and certified personal trainers who are intimately familiar with this fan bike.
  • At Breaking Muscle, we know exercise equipment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Assault Bike ProX is one of the best cardio machines presently offered, as it provides a full-body, low-impact workout that can still be high-intensity. Popular in the CrossFit community, this fan bike consists of a belt-driven system and a heavy-duty steel frame, making it a great tool to build both endurance and strength.

It has been revealed that here at Breaking Muscle, our experts include athletes, strength and conditioning coaches, and certified personal trainers who are intimately familiar with this fan bike. We put it through hours of strenuous cardio workouts to see if it could take on the challenge. In this Assault Fitness AssaultBike Pro X review, we’ll highlight our results, how well the bike ranked in testing, and how it compares to other fan bikes.

At Breaking Muscle, we know exercise equipment. We have a product testing team that has put hundreds of machines through the wringer, using them for everything from gentle warm-ups to high-intensity interval training (HIIT) workouts. Many of our staff members are home gym owners themselves and use these products nearly every day.

With the knowledge we’ve gained over the years, we created a proprietary scoring system that we used to rank the AssaultBike ProX in various categories. Not only did we evaluate how the bike performed on its own, but we also compared it with nearly 30 other exercise bikes to see how it stacked up against the competition.

From the founders of the AssaultRunner (one of the best treadmills to train with), the Assault Bike ProX is made with a heavy-duty steel frame finished in a black powder coat that helps keep it corrosion-resistant and capable of standing the test of time. It is a top-tier fan bike that can provide a brutal workout for any athlete.

In addition to its tough and durable frame, it incorporates a belt-driven system for a quiet, smooth training experience. It also requires less upkeep than chain-driven systems, which should come as a relief to busy individuals who can’t be bothered with complicated maintenance protocols.

It has been revealed that at the time of writing, the Assault Bike ProX costs $899. Fortunately, there is also an option to finance it at around $82 a month through Affirm. For comparison, the Assault Bike ProX is more expensive than the AssaultBike Classic at $699 but cheaper than the Concept2 BikeErg, which costs around $1,100.

The Assault Bike ProX also provides free shipping, which is a major deal for equipment this size. Buying an air bike from another brand could set you back another $100 in shipping costs.

All of the above considered, we’ve rated this bike 4 out of 5 stars for its shipping rate, finance options, and value.

It has been revealed that the Assault Bike ProX weighs 125 pounds, has a max user weight of 330 pounds, and boasts a heavy-duty steel frame with a corrosion-resistant black powder coating finish. We love this type of frame and finish because it means less maintenance over time.

It’s also similar to what you would see with the Rogue Echo Bike, which has a black powder coating and almost looks like it was built from scraps of a heavy-duty squat rack! But the Assault Bike ProX isn’t as bulky as the Rogue Echo Bike, making it more compatible with small spaces, which our product testers enjoyed. For comparison, the ProX is 51.73 inches long, 24.52 inches wide, and 52.51 inches high, while the Echo Bike is 55 inches long, 29.5 inches wide, and 52.25 inches high.

Sources indicate that the Assault Bike ProX provides a wide padded seat that can adjust to 11 different heights and six different directions either forward or backward. These adjustments were the same on the Assault Bike Pro, which the ProX replaces. The rubber handles on the ProX help you maintain your grip and keep your hands comfortable throughout the workout as well.

This fan bike also comes with footpegs at the base of the handlebars for you to place your feet. This gives you the option to do an upper body-only workout, which is great for injury recovery or arm day.

Based on the quality and construction of the Assault Bike ProX, we rated it 5 out of 5 stars.

We gave the AssaultBike Pro X 5 out of 5 stars for delivery and assembly because of how straightforward it was to build. The bikes arrived at our testing facility 75 percent built, so all we had to do was attach the LCD console, pedals, handlebars, seat post, and saddle. Assault Fitness provides all the tools needed to build your air bike, and it should take roughly 35 to 45 minutes.

It has been revealed that when testing the Assault Bike ProX, we noticed a smoother and quieter ride than what we’ve experienced with other air bikes, like the Titan Fan Bike or the AssaultBike Classic. This is predominantly thanks to the belt-driven system. A belt-driven system requires less maintenance than a chain-driven system, but it is also harder to use. When you pedal, the steel fan wheel generates resistance based on your effort. The harder you pedal, the more resistance is applied.

However, once you stop pedaling, the fan wheel will stop moving, requiring more effort to get it started again. This might be tough if you’re not prepared for a high-intensity workout. Due to this, we gave the Assault Bike ProX a 4 out of 5-star rating for performance.

The Assault Bike ProX’s LCD monitor provides seven built-in training programs and a competition mode for those ready to take on the challenge. Through the Assault Fitness App, which we’ll review below, there is also an option to follow instructor-led programs or create customized workouts.

All in all, we give it a 3 out of 5 star rating in this category. The included workouts aren’t as robust as what you’d see in a more interactive bike like the Peloton. However, we do appreciate having them and think they can be valuable for people who may not know where to start.

Recent findings suggest that while the AssaultBike Classic was only compatible with the Polar T34 heart rate chest strap, the Assault Bike ProX is compatible with other brands, like Garmin. You can link a heart rate monitor through the bike’s Bluetooth features. However, you need to purchase a compatible one separately, which is why we only rated it 4 out of 5 stars here (though to be fair, this is common for most exercise bikes).

The Assault Bike ProX comes with a five-inch by eight-inch monitor, which is a common size amongst other fan bikes. This high-quality LCD monitor is powered by four AA batteries, which Assault includes with your purchase. The console is great for tracking stats such as calories, distance, heart rate, speed, watts, and RPM. It also connects to the Assault Fitness App.

Our product testers loved that it could track power output in addition to distance and speed, which is a great measure of energy expenditure to quantify workout intensity. The Rogue Echo Bike monitor doesn’t provide feedback such as watts and RPM on its monitor, which gives the Assault Bike ProX the edge.

All things considered, we’ve given this bike 5 out of 5 stars for its display and tracking capabilities.

Industry observers note that when testing the Assault Bike ProX, we noticed a ton of conveniences. First, the air bike requires no electric outlet, and we loved being able to use it anywhere. This feature is also a welcome benefit for commercial CrossFit gym owners, as you don’t have to worry about your members tripping over power cords.

According to recent reports, other conveniences include a device holder and a water bottle holder. Some fan bikes like the Titan Fan Bike also include these conveniences. Others, like the Rogue Echo Bike, don’t (though they are available to purchase separately). We always appreciate it when a brand throws in little extras like this. They allow you to have all your workout essentials within reach. Plus, you don’t have to worry about potentially placing multiple orders or paying extra shipping fees to get them.

Sources indicate that overall, our product testers rated the conveniences 4 out of 5 stars. The only reason we docked a point is that we wish the bike came with a wind guard to prevent cold air from blowing in our faces when training in a cold garage. There is one available on the Assault Fitness website, but you have to buy it separately for an additional $39.

It has been revealed that the Assault Bike ProX is a part of the Assault Fitness line of exercise machines that operate using the Assault Fitness app. The app was one of our product testers’ favorite features.

According to recent reports, free to download from the App Store and Google Play, the Assault Fitness App provides you with a multitude of instructor-driven workouts. You can do these workouts on your own or compete against other athletes virtually. Many of the workouts also integrate other types of equipment, such as dumbbells and kettlebells, to help you get more well-rounded programming.

While we enjoyed the app, we only gave it 4 out of 5 stars. As of this writing, it’s not available on the most recent version of Android. Athletes with newer Android phones may not be able to use it.

Industry observers note that the Assault Bike ProX is Bluetooth-enabled. We don’t necessarily consider Bluetooth connectivity a standout feature, as dozens of cardio machines we’ve tested now come with it. But we’ve also tried inexpensive cardio equipment that doesn’t have this feature, and even Assault Fitness’s classic AssaultBike lacks Bluetooth capabilities. As such, we rated the ProX 5 out of 5 stars here.

It has been revealed that when comparing other fan bikes we tested, the Assault Bike ProX generated less noise due to its belt-driven system. The belt-driven system operates more smoothly than chain-drive systems such as those on the Schwinn Airdyne. A noisier system can make it tough to perform workouts at home, especially if you train early in the morning or late at night when others are sleeping.

Recent findings suggest that that remarked, no fan bike will be completely silent, so you should still expect some noise as air travels through the flywheel. Due to this, we give the noise level of the Assault Bike ProX 4 out of 5 stars.

The Assault Bike ProX offers some portability, thanks to two small transport wheels at the front. To move it, all you need to do is tilt it onto its wheels to help glide it across the floor. However, although it might be easy for some athletes to move this fan bike, others might struggle to relocate it because it weighs 125 pounds. Based on these findings, we give the portability of the Assault Bike ProX 4 out of 5 stars.

The Assault Bike ProX has a three-year non-wear parts warranty and a seven-year frame warranty. The three-year non-wear parts warranty doesn’t cover normal wear and tear on parts like the seat, pedals, and handle grips. This may seem like a drawback, but in our experience, this is common in warranties on other brands’ fan bikes. But the length of Assault’s warranty is longer compared to Rogue, who only offers a two-year warranty on their Echo Bike, and Titan, who only offers a one-year warranty on their fan bike. We gave the warranty of the Assault Bike ProX 5 out of 5 stars for this reason.

The Assault Bike ProX is 51.73 inches long, 24.52 inches wide, and 52.51 inches high. Compared to the classic AssaultBike, these dimensions are one to two inches bigger in each category. If you’re between the two, we definitely recommend measuring carefully to ensure you choose the one that will best fit your space.

It has been revealed that the Assault Bike ProX is a fan bike, meaning it builds resistance based on how much air you recruit in the fan wheel as you work. The harder you pedal, the more air resistance is applied, making your workout more challenging.

In addition to air resistance, the ProX uses a belt-driven system, meaning it only operates when you begin to pedal. If you stop pedaling, the machine stops moving. This makes it harder to operate compared to a chair-driven system, like what you’d see with the AssaultBike Classic.

The weight capacity of the Assault Bike ProX is 330 pounds. This is more than the Classic bike, which holds 300 pounds, but less than the Elite, which holds up to 350 pounds.

It has been revealed that the Assault Bike ProX can accommodate most body sizes with 11 different height settings and six front-to-back settings. These adjustment levels are relatively standard based on what we’ve seen on other fan bikes. However, some competitors like the Rogue Echo Bike only have five front-to-back seat settings.

Because the Assault Bike ProX does not require an electrical outlet, you can transport it wherever you want to go —outdoors or indoors. The monitor, however, does require AA batteries to operate.

At first glance, it seems the Assault Bike ProX and Rogue Echo Bike have many similarities. When you analyze them more closely, you’ll find that there are several key differences between the two.

Below are the dimensions of both fan bikes:.

Even though the Rogue Echo Bike is bulkier in material and dimensions, it has the same 330-pound weight capacity as the AssaultBike ProX. Both of these fan bikes are also powered by movement, so no electrical outlet is needed. Further, weighing in at 123 and 125 pounds, respectively, the Rogue Echo Bike and the Assault Bike ProX are equally portable, especially given they both have wheels.

Finally, both products use belt-driven mechanics, providing a smooth and quiet riding experience. But the Assault Bike ProX gives more metrics on the monitor, such as watts and RPM. This feature alone could make or break your decision, depending on how important tracking is to your training.

Sources indicate that the Assault Bike ProX comes in with a strong 4.6 out of 5-star rating on the Assault Fitness website. Many people claim that it is super easy to set up, requires low maintenance, and is a favorite piece of equipment in their home gyms. Customers also praise its sturdiness and its ability to handle a tough workout.

According to recent reports, one user mentioned that the left peg became loose during their workout. Another buyer mentioned that the Assault Bike ProX was very noisy and didn’t think it was as stable as other reviews might suggest — note, however, that complaints like this are in the minority.

According to recent reports, after extensive research and testing of the Assault Bike ProX, we can say that this air bike is worth it. Made with a heavy-duty steel frame finished in a black powder coat, it can take on the toughest workouts. It’s ideal for anyone looking for a full-body, high-intensity interval training machine for improving both endurance and strength.

According to recent reports, the smoother and quieter experience you get with the Assault Bike ProX is thanks to the belt-driven system integrated into the design. Although this system might require more effort to operate, this bike can still be a great purchase for everyone from CrossFitters to health and fitness enthusiasts.

Industry observers note that the Assault Bike provides a great workout, combining air resistance and a belt-driven system for a tough cardio and muscular endurance workout. You can use both the foot pedals and the arm handles to get a full-body workout. Or you can just use the arm handles to work out your upper body exclusively.

Recent findings suggest that the Assault Bike Pro X is a belt-driven system. The fan bike only works when you operate the pedals and/or handlebars. The belt-driven system also offers a smoother and quieter workout.

Recent findings suggest that the AssaultBike alone may not aid fat loss if you’re eating too many calories. However,  it can provide a strong enough stimulus for an intense enough workout to help you burn more calories and hit multiple health and fitness goals.

Because the AssaultBike Pro X requires a full-body effort and utilizes a belt-driven system, you could potentially build a small amount of muscle by using it consistently. However, resistance training with implements like dumbbells or barbells (and following a diet that supports muscle growth) will be your best bet if you want to pack on as much muscle as possible.

For Years, Doctors Blamed My Mysterious Symptoms on Running. A Simple Blood Test Proved Them Wrong.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article originally appeared in the Spring 2025 matter of Runner’s World.
  • Running and menstruation entered my life around the same time, at age 13.
  • Throughout my years on the high school cross-country team, this irregular pattern stuck: I only got about four periods a year and never knew when they would arrive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article originally appeared in the Spring 2025 matter of Runner’s World.

Running and menstruation entered my life around the same time, at age 13. I got hooked on running the mile, and, swayed by a persistent and impactful track coach, I eventually left soccer behind to join the cross-country team. My first period arrived right before my first track season; however, while the training cycles progressed, my menstrual cycle didn’t—my second period wouldn’t come until five months later.

Throughout my years on the high school cross-country team, this irregular pattern stuck: I only got about four periods a year and never knew when they would arrive. I felt confused and left out whenever my teammates asked me for a menstrual pad I had no use for, like my body couldn’t do what it was supposed to do.

It has been revealed that when it came to running, though, my body felt strong, capable of carrying me through interval workouts and lifting heavy weights during weight room sessions. On the track, I felt more equal to my teammates. The training cycle was one I could control.

According to recent reports, at my yearly physical exams, I expressed concern that my periods weren’t occurring monthly, and the feedback was the same every time: I was still young, and sometimes it takes time to become regular. That I accepted. What didn’t sit well with me was what followed: “You’re missing periods because you run a lot. Try eating more.”.

Neither felt like an answer to the problem. My 20-something-mile weeks kept me physically fit and helped me deal with anxiety, especially when my dysfunctional home life felt out of control. Not only did the exam show I kept a healthy weight, I had been putting on muscle mass from deadlifting 200 pounds. But hoping the doctor was right, I took a year off from distance training.

Still, no regular cycle in sight.

Sources indicate that at 19, I started seeing a new primary care physician. My doctor was surprised when I recounted my prior experiences. “So you’ve never had any blood tests done?” they asked. I underwent the test and a pelvic ultrasound, and it didn’t take very long to get an answer: The likely culprit was polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).

Industry observers note that PCOS is the most common endocrine disorder in people assigned female at birth of reproductive age, yet so much about the condition is still unknown, including the cause of PCOS, according to the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. The National Institutes of Health requires only two of the following symptoms for PCOS diagnosis (all of which I’ve experienced): ovulatory dysfunction (irregular, heavy, or missed periods), high androgen levels (often manifesting as excessive body hair or acne), and/or one or more cysts on the ovaries. Besides irregular menstruation, PCOS can cause, for example, infertility and weight gain. Although there isn’t a permanent cure, some patients are able to treat their symptoms by managing their lifestyle: eating well, exercising regularly, and getting enough sleep.

It has been revealed that the diagnosis came at a turbulent time in my life. I was swept up in another cycle: emotional abuse stemming from controlling relationships. I escaped this abuse through schoolwork and decided to take extra classes over the summer so I could graduate from college a year early and find my own place.

But I also got back to running, which has always helped me build a sense of agency and played a big role in my postgrad transition—I spent that summer running across the empty campus and habitually relying on a few miles to calm me when faced with chaos. I started taking an herbal supplement that others with PCOS raved about. I moved in with roommates. I found a therapist to help me unpack the trauma I’ve experienced.

And at 21, I finally started to get a regular monthly period.

Every menstruation since has felt like Christmas morning…followed by some gnawing cramps.

What I am only now starting to understand is just how much my environment affected my mental health and how that in turn impacted my physical health. I recently read research studies linking PCOS and emotional abuse, and that’s when I found what felt like the last missing link.

I still mourn for the runner I was in high school, who felt lost and frustrated without any answers, dealing with conflicting feelings around her body image. I remember lying on cold, uncomfortable tables, intimidated by informational pamphlets—none of which covered hormonal health—all while doctors were delivering confusing medical advice or dismissing my concerns with oversimplified notions. A 2022 health survey found that 29 percent of women and 21 percent of men felt doctors disregarded their worries during visits. I was told my problem existed “because I ran.” In reality, it’s far more complex than what many people are told, and I am just one example.

According to recent reports, I’ve since run two half marathons while maintaining regular periods throughout each training cycle. Running was never the problem. On the contrary, the very thing doctors blamed my symptoms on brought me relief all along—and I will never give it up again.

It has been revealed that kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and presently competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.
