📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

From 55 degrees down to 25, I bring one piece of cold-weather gear on every ride: a neck buff. It isn’t the most exciting item in my kit, and it won’t make a dramatic difference in a gear photo. But it’s useful across a wider range of temperatures than almost anything else I own, and it costs far less than most winter gear cyclists spend serious money on.

At 55 degrees, I can wear it loosely around my neck and cut the wind without feeling bundled up. As the temperature drops, that little bit of insulation becomes more valuable. Covering your neck makes you feel warmer, and the buff also helps close the gap at the top of your jacket. Cold air sneaking in around the collar can make an otherwise reasonable layering setup feel inadequate. A buff helps keep that draft out.

In a recent development, when it gets really cold, I pull it up over my ears and face. It’s a simple way to add coverage without committing to a heavier balaclava for the whole ride. And if the temperature changes, or I start working harder on a climb, I can pull it back down in a few seconds. It takes up almost no space in a jersey pocket, which means there’s little reason to leave it at home.

According to recent reports, neck buffs grew out of a practical problem familiar to motorcycle riders: keeping cold, wind, and road dust off your neck and face. Riders already used bandanas and other neck cloths; the stretchy tube made that protection easier to wear under a helmet. Skiers adopted it too, which may be why people associate it with snow sports.

Industry observers note that there is no shortage of expensive cycling accessories that promise to keep you warm while riding. Many are quite good. But few come close to the humble neck buff in terms of how practical, simple, and cheap it is. It’s an adaptable piece of kit that’s just as useful on a cool ride that doesn’t quite call for full winter kit as it is on a truly cold ride, when every gap and exposed bit of skin becomes a problem. It’s a small thing, which is exactly why I never leave home without it.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but promptly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

According to recent reports, editor’s Note, November 20, 2026: There are several markdowns on our list for Black Friday! The hi-vis and reflective Headsweats Cap and Nathan Run Cool Stash Hat are both 25% off. Scroll down for even more hats on sale!

You won’t catch me heading out for a run without a hat. Unlike headbands, which tend to slip over my eyes or off my head, caps stay put and have a long list of features that optimize your run. The whole point of a hat is to make my runs easier.

When I’m shopping for the perfect hat, it has to check off several boxes:.

The hat completes my race outfit when I’m running any distance from a mile to a marathon. It keeps my hair from getting into my eyes, and sometimes has extra features, like UPF or even a pocket. And with brands making hats with cool patterns, it can also be a vessel for self-expression. They know that wearing a favorite accessory, one that puts the fun in functionality, can get you into the right headspace when you run.

Sources indicate that I started wearing running hats seven years ago. I’m so used to wearing a hat on a run that I feel naked running without one. As I accumulated hats, I started to see some fits and features trumped others. The hats on this list were evaluated with years of experience, research, and hat testing.

On top of my own research, I also had some of our RW staffers test caps and provide feedback.

The caps below all have features that cater to different needs and types of runs. From logging a run on a blistering hot day, going for a workout in the evening, or having a penchant for snacking on pickles during training, know this: there’s a hat for that.

I’ve also added some beanies for the colder months. When testing beanies, I paid attention to fit, comfort, and warmth. It’s not true that you’ll catch cold if your head isn’t covered, but that doesn’t mean you shouldn’t wear a hat to keep your cool.

The Ciele FSTCap wins Best Overall as a cap-wearing runner because of its no-fuss, flexible design. The brim isn’t rigid, allowing it to sit comfortably on your head, and it doesn’t flop out of shape. It’s lightweight and breathable, with fast-drying, anti-odor mesh panels.

But its best feature is the adjustable bungee cord closure. I’ve worn several iterations of Ciele FSTCap at races, and the simplicity of the hat gives me peace of mind before racing because the toggle doesn’t require much dexterity when my arms feel like Jell-O during a marathon when I have to loosen or tighten the cord. It’s machine-washable, too.

Industry observers note that this hat is Best Budget, but it’s also Best Visibility. The entire rim of this Headsweats’s Hat has reflective trim for visibility in low light, making a car’s lights heighten your bobbing cap’s outline when you’re running on the shoulder at dusk or dawn, or even nighttime. This feature is fantastic if you feel the neon colors are a little too loud to your liking. The black version isn’t a bad choice, thanks to the reflective rim.

The hat is a great tool when you’re an early riser or night owl, and the knit shell is soft and breathable. I do have one main critique: it looks cheaply made. I can get over the knit material wearing fast—proper care, like machine washing and air-drying only, should add to the cap’s longevity. Maybe it’s the lack of patterns or even mesh panels or overlays besides the logo on the side. While this hat doesn’t win fashion contests, it definitely fulfills its purpose for running safely by staying visible.

Recent findings suggest that the Ponyflo Alex Active was tested by me and editor Monique LeBrun, who noted we should add this hat to our guide for runners who specifically wear high hairstyles. The positioning of the pony opening allows you to run without your visor comically almost covering your eyes if your hair is half-braided high. Runners like me will appreciate how the positioning makes my hair stop just above my back so it’s not whipping my back when I run.

Recent findings suggest that the hat comes in a variety of colors and there’s even an edition with a longer, wider brim for more sun coverage; though both LeBrun and I felt like we were about to spend a day out gardening wearing them. We felt the brim on the Alex Active sufficed, but the option is there.

In a recent development, even though the Ciele FSTCap is my racing hat of choice, we’re giving the best racing hat accolade to the Rnnr Pacer Hat. Our testers loved how feather-light the Pacer is and how its perforated panels provide ultimate ventilation.

My one knock would be the buckle, but we didn’t find ourselves struggling to adjust the closure.

“I suppose the best thing I can say about this hat is that never once did I have to adjust it midrun,” remarked RW News Director Andrew Daniels, who tested the whimsically graphic Jungalow version.

According to recent reports, our other Pacer tester, News Editor Theo Kahler, chose to wear the less loud, mostly black Bolt iteration. He appreciated how the hat wasn’t bulky or stiff. “It didn’t give me headaches like some hats do,” he said. But he had one complaint: “On the inside, it claims ‘Party pace wins the race.’ I don’t really know what that means and could personally do without that.” And as Scroogy as the comment may have sounded, I got a kick out of that.

A pocket in a hat is hard to find, so I was glad to stumble across Nathan’s Run Cool Stash. The hidden pocket can doubly serve as storage space for ice, a key, or even an ID card. The pocket is drop-in below and above; I can tuck in my ID card in both flaps, or clip on a running light. It’s a close stretch against your head so items won’t bounce in the compartment as you run. It’s perfect for my key fob when I park my car by a trail, and can’t store it in my pocket-free shorts.

One caveat: you can only stash on one side of the hat, so if you’re feeling the heat on your right side, I guess you’ll have to wear the cap backwards to cool that side down.

All hail the hard-brimmed trucker hat—only Oiselle does theirs with a twist. The firm brim folds in half down the center, making it easy to downsize into a little triangle and stash into your pocket if you want the sun to hit your face (or maybe have that hat rim forehead imprint fade before you head to work in the morning).

Recent findings suggest that this was the only hat I packed when I stayed in Sydney for a week leading up to the marathon. The interior sweatband’s mantra “Go fast, take chances” was the positive energy I needed running a race on the opposite side of the world. The wide-holed mesh back also kept my head cool as the race went on and the day got warmer.

A small drawback is how funky the hat can get after a couple wears. The hat is hand-wash only, which explains why an old Runner Trucker’s toggle broke after a machine wash. The hat is mighty on the run, but delicate during a wash cycle.

I’m going on five years running in my Pickle Peeps hat and have had several compliments over the years whenever I wore it. The all-over print of smiling, shades-wearing dills, gherkins, and cornichons helps me take my races not too seriously. And I’ll absolutely use this hat as an unvoiced request to have the pickle that comes with your sandwich during a postrun brunch.

Sources indicate that I loved this hat so much, I called a Barnes & Noble in Dallas, Texas, to find it and please mail it back when I realized I returned home without my Pickle Peeps in tow. But it’s not just this hat: bananas, ice cream, flying pigs, pizza slices—I have a Sprints hat for every craving and every mood.

Sources indicate that my only critique is the Velcro closure. It’s ruined running shirts, scarves, and whatever else is in my laundry basket or accessories pile. Sprints has snapbacks, but they don’t come in an extensive pattern collection. Sometimes I have to safety-pin the closure when the humidity puffs out my hair.

Industry observers note that the Varsity Runner’s Hat brings to mind snowy winters on campus when I went to college in New England. The hat stays put when I head out on windy winter runs, and functions as an out-and-about beanie when I’m not running. The 100-percent merino wool material helps with thermoregulation and sweat-wicking.

The Creek Run Beanie’s waffle knit texture screams cozy, but you can also wear it when you’re actually running (as its name suggests), or skiing if that’s also your thing during the winter. This hat is stretchy but it does run small.

Recent findings suggest that the Skida Alpine is a stretchy, toasty hat that doesn’t overheat your head. Senior Editor Cat Bowen appreciated how the hat was sensory-friendly; its material feels super smooth, and it requires no tugging or micro-adjusting.

Fit can sometimes be tricky when the hat you’re interested in is unisex, or the over-confidently phrased “one size fits all.” You want the hat to be secure around your head so it doesn’t fly off on windy runs, but not too tight that you get a headache.

Sources indicate that if the hat comes in multiple sizes, peruse the site’s fit instructions to match. If it’s the dreaded OSFA, check the type of adjustability and material to make sure it stretches and it can expand—or tighten—around your crown.

Recent findings suggest that concerning caps, you have plenty of options to consider in terms of adjustability and closures. Velcro allows you to easily adjust without fumbling with toggles or buckles and straps, but the material isn’t stretchy and can lose its adhesiveness. Buckles/snaps stay put but can be a pain to troubleshoot and aren’t always easy to adjust midrun.

My personal favorite is the bungee toggle, but they don’t always lock in place and the cord can overstretch over time.

I’m the owner of several hats and no matter how much I rotate or wash them, they eventually get funky. Besides retiring old hats or soaking them in vinegar and baking soda, one thing that doesn’t draw flies to my head postrun is perforated panels or mesh on my cap.

In a recent development, material is also key, especially when it comes to beanies. Instead of the inevitable sauna your head would be subjected to running in a rigid, cotton-canvas trucker hat, technical running caps are made of nylon and polyester, and beanies are made of polyester and merino wool, which evaporate moisture by drying fast.

Any ol’ running hat, IMHO, is better than none, but there are hats with extra features to look for if you want a hat more tailored to your needs. Some hats come with UPF to block UVB and UVA rays. Reflective detail is something to consider if your runs are mostly in low light. Pockets are great for storing small items, like a key or even a photo ID if you’re okay with running with a noticeable rectangle on the side of your head. I sure am.

How do I measure my head to get my hat size?

According to recent reports, the circumference around your head, above your eyebrows and ears is the measurement you seek. You can use a tape measure, or string and ruler if you don’t have measuring tape, to find your circumference. Then, check the brand’s sizing, if provided, to find your fit.

Does running in a cap make you warmer?

This depends on the thinness of the material and the breathability features—is it mesh, perforated? Some caps like the Nathan Cool Stash Hat can store cold packs or ice in a pocket. An easy way to keep your head cool is to dunk your hat in cold water before heading out on a run. And to keep your head warm? Go with a hat made of merino wool, which naturally insulates.

It has been revealed that amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

Cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Holding multiple advanced degrees and presently studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. Passionate about women’s health and neurodivergent inclusion, she advocates for closing research gaps and helping others—especially AudHD people—find joy in running and fitness.

XWERKS Motion BCAA Review (2025): A Registered Dietitian’s Honest Thoughts

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, your gym bag is probably packed with some of the best supplements for building muscle, including protein powder, creatine, and pre-workout.
  • Enter XWERKS Motion — an innovative supplement formulated to enhance endurance during intense exercise and support a quick post-workout recovery.
  • Our team of personal trainers, CrossFit coaches, nutrition experts, and competitive weightlifters shared their feedback on the formulation, price, taste, and solubility of this one-of-a-kind product.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, your gym bag is probably packed with some of the best supplements for building muscle, including protein powder, creatine, and pre-workout. Crucial for boosting energy and strength during a gym session and reducing muscle soreness afterward, you wouldn’t dare train without them. But imagine a single supplement that combines the benefits of all three.

Enter XWERKS Motion — an innovative supplement formulated to enhance endurance during intense exercise and support a quick post-workout recovery. Sounds too good to be true? We’ll find out in this XWERKS Motion review.

Our team of personal trainers, CrossFit coaches, nutrition experts, and competitive weightlifters shared their feedback on the formulation, price, taste, and solubility of this one-of-a-kind product. As a registered dietitian nutritionist, I’ll do a deep dive into the ingredients and potential health benefits of XWERKS Motion, so you know if it’s worth adding to your supplement stack.

In a recent development, medical disclaimer: This article is intended for educational and informational purposes only. It is not intended as a substitute for medical advice. For health advice, contact a licensed healthcare provider.

Our Breaking Muscle product testing team has tried nearly 20 of the best BCAA supplements, gaining a thorough understanding of what meets customer standards and what falls short. Here’s how our expert testers rated the following categories after trying XWERKS Motion themselves.

According to recent reports, in this XWERKS Motion review, we’ll explore the product’s cost, formula, flavors, taste, and more. We’ll include honest, reliable feedback straight from our Breaking Muscle expert testers, so you’ll know exactly what to expect from this supplement. With transparency in mind, we include the good and not-so-good aspects of XWERKS Motion to give you the full picture.

Sources indicate that in comparison, Transparent Labs BCAA Glutamine costs $1.33 per serving, while Jacked Factory BCAA Powder is available at $0.67 per serving at the time of this writing. XWERKS Motion is on the pricier side, earning this category a 3.5 out of 5, but also contains ingredients not found in most other BCAA supplements.

According to recent reports, XWERKS Motion is thoughtfully and originally formulated, earning it a 4 out of 5. It is unlike other BCAA supplements in that it contains 25 grams of cluster dextrin carbohydrates, also known as highly branched cyclic dextrin (HBCD). Cluster dextrin passes through the stomach into the intestines rapidly, where it can be absorbed into the bloodstream and taken up into muscle cells to replenish glycogen content and provide a quick energy source. (1).

In a recent development, human studies suggest that when used before or during a workout, cluster dextrin carbs may decrease perceived exertion and enhance endurance when compared to maltodextrin and glucose, especially when prior carb intake is low. (1) However, those who eat plenty of carbs may not experience any added benefits when supplementing cluster dextrin.

In addition to carbs, each serving offers three grams of branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs). The product contains the BCAA ratio 2:1:1 of leucine, isoleucine, and valine. BCAAs are essential amino acids (EAAs), meaning you must consume them because the body doesn’t synthesize them on its own. Leucine is often thought of as the king of BCAAs because it activates muscle protein synthesis, which is necessary for muscle growth and recovery. (2).

In a recent development, other active ingredients include calcium, magnesium, and sodium. During exercise, you lose electrolytes through sweat that need to be replenished. The electrolytes in XWERKS Motion help prevent dehydration and maintain proper muscle function during a workout.

Enhanced with natural flavors, sucralose, and citric acid, this product contains ingredients that add sour and sweet notes.

Sucralose is an artificial sweetener considered safe when consumed in moderation. Unlike table sugar, most research indicates sucralose has little to no effects on blood sugar levels or insulin. (3) However, some animal studies suggest it could disrupt healthy gut bacteria and increase inflammation when consumed long-term, but more human studies are needed. (4).

You won’t have any difficulty picking a flavor if you choose to try XWERKS Motion, considering there is only one option available — Raspberry Lemonade. Obviously, if you prefer to stick with one flavor on repeat this won’t be a problem. For those who like to switch things up, the lack of variety may leave you feeling bored, hence the middle-of-the-road rating on flavor.

Luckily, the Raspberry Lemonade flavor delivers. Our expert tester was more than pleased with the taste of the raspberry lemonade supplement, rating it an impressive 5 out of 5. She noticed hints of the tart lemonade with a more robust berry flavor overall. The supplement wasn’t too sweet and had a very refreshing taste to it. Our tester even went as far as to say that she could happily sip on this drink all day.

Another winning category of XWERKS Motion is solubility, which our tester rated a perfect 5 out of 5. She didn’t experience any clumping, grittiness, floaties, or difficulty mixing — a feature you’ll want when drinking it at the gym or on the go. Because the cluster dextrin in this product is highly soluble in water, it dissolves easily and forms a smooth, uniform mixture. Several customer reviews on the XWERKS website rave about the product’s superior solubility, mentioning it “blends so smooth” and is “easy to mix.”.

Cluster dextrin is believed to be safe for consumption, with no apparent safety concerns. (5) Our product tester didn’t experience any adverse side effects during her use of this product. As for beneficial effects, she didn’t notice any superhuman strength or noticeable bursts of energy, but she did feel good during longer lifting sessions.

Switching gears, BCAAs are considered safe when consumed in appropriate dosages. It’s best to adhere to the suggested dosage instructions on the product label for optimal safety and effectiveness.

According to recent reports, nevertheless, always consult with your healthcare provider before adding a fresh dietary supplement to your routine, particularly if you have pre-existing medical conditions or are presently taking prescribed medications. This precaution ensures that the supplement aligns with your individual health needs and won’t pose any risks or interactions.

All of the above considered, XWERKS Motion gets a 4 out of 5 rating for the lack of side effects from its formulation.

Unfortunately, there’s no mention of third-party testing on the XWERKS Motion product page, which is why we gave it a 1 out of 5.

We always encourage consumers to consider supplements that are third-party tested, because it serves as a quality control measure, ensuring that products are safe, effective, and meet certain regulatory requirements. Third-party testing enhances transparency and builds consumer trust by verifying that high-quality products contain what’s on the label and don’t include harmful levels of heavy metals or contaminants.

Sources indicate that XWERKS Motion and XTEND Original BCAA powder have both commonalities and differences. To start, both products contain BCAAs and electrolytes to enhance muscle recovery, reduce muscle soreness, and maintain hydration.

However, that’s where their similarities end. While XTEND Original BCAA powder doesn’t contain any carbohydrates, XWERKS Motion contains 25 grams of cluster dextrin carbs for extra energy and prolonged endurance.

Industry observers note that XTEND Original BCAA powder also has a much higher BCAA content of seven grams, compared to the three grams in XWERKS Motion. The Original BCAA powder even contains a whopping three and a half grams of leucine, exceeding the recommended two to three grams per day to maximize muscle-gaining capabilities. (2) The same can’t be noted for the leucine content of XWERKS Motion.

It has been revealed that customers on the XWERKS website give Motion a 4.4 out of 5-star rating. There are only 35 reviews on the product page. Motion is not available on Amazon at the time of writing.

Sources indicate that one happy customer says, “Great taste! No challenges with digestion, gives you the fuel needed during most intense workouts.” Another customer says, “It mixes well, I like the flavor, and have no digestive or other issues. Performance-wise I feel great. I feel more energetic during my workouts and that I’m getting more out of them.”.

In a recent development, reviews from customers who were less pleased with the product were written over a year ago, and the formulation and flavors may have changed. One customer notes, “I’m not sold on this product. I don’t really notice any difference on the days I take this. Also, it takes a blender to get this stuff mixed! That’s a deal breaker for me.” Other customers complain of the grape flavor, which is no longer available.

According to recent reports, XWERKS Motion provides a synergistic blend of cluster dextrin carbs, BCAAs, and electrolytes to support endurance and recovery during and after a workout. Those who enjoy leisurely activity and consume enough carbs to sustain their energy levels may not benefit from this product.

However, it might be worth it for endurance athletes and bodybuilders with high training loads. Taking XWERKS before, during, or after intense physical activity may reduce perceived effort, extend the time to exhaustion, and decrease muscle soreness.

You can consume BCAAs pre, post, or intra-workout depending on your fitness goals. Some prefer to take BCAAs before or during a workout to provide their muscles with amino acids to help prevent muscle protein breakdown. Others like to take BCAAs post-workout to support muscle repair and recovery.

According to recent reports, if you eat a whole-food diet high in protein, then you likely consume enough amino acids and may not experience further benefits by supplementing them. If you struggle to eat enough protein, BCAAs may support endurance, helping you train at a higher intensity for longer. Additionally, BCAAs may reduce muscle damage and DOMS post-workout.

It has been revealed that BCAAs are a group of three EEAs—leucine, isoleucine, and valine— that must be consumed through the diet. They get their name from their unique molecular structure. While all EAAs are key, BCAAs are thought to play an important role in protein synthesis, muscle recovery, and preventing loss of lean mass.

Sources indicate that BCAAs may provide an extended feeling of energy and delay the onset of muscle fatigue, enabling you to work out longer. Moreover, BCAAs might diminish muscle damage, inflammation, and DOMS post-workout. Lastly, BCAAs may aid in preserving lean muscle mass during periods of fat loss, contributing to weight loss efforts.

It has been revealed that there are no official recommended daily requirements for BCAAs. The suggested sweet spot for leucine intake is often cited as two to three grams per day to optimize muscle building. (2) Avoid exceeding the recommended serving size on the product label. If you take protein powder or eat a high-protein diet, BCAA supplements likely won’t provide added benefits.

If these aren’t in my stocking this year, I will be sending my husband the “I got a robe” skit from SNL every hour on the hour until New Years. These are too perfect. They’re not socks for running, but they are runner’s socks. You know?

We know ourselves enough to laugh at ourselves. Also, why are there no ultra versions of this one? Because I ran an ultra, dangit.

Trying to keep a headband up is a pain in the butt. This band stays up, keeps ears warm and cozy, and doesn’t itch, which is the most important bit. It’s super stretchy, but a toss in the wash brings it back to rights if it gets a bit stretched out.

Industry observers note that muscle cramps suck. Full stop. But magnesium spray helps. This is my personal favorite. I used it after my last ultra, and this, with some heat and massage? Magic.

Let us not mince words—runners’ feet can be pretty gnarly. If you’re running for 10, 15, or 26.2 miles at a time, they’re going to take a beating. This kit comes with a pumice powder soap to help smooth the feet, a peppermint lotion for revitalization, and a foot balm to really get in there and start healing those cracks and calluses.

Industry observers note that runners love socks. We just do. Stick ‘em in our stockings, wrap them under the tree, hand them to us passing in the hall, we’re happy. We love these because they help prevent blisters and they’re oh-so-comfy for long runs.

These shorts are really special. They’re a lined short with a light, breezy, bicycle short under the flowy top piece that has real pockets! You’re getting chafing protection and the modesty from the flowy outer short. They’re breathable and they come to just the right place on the belly.

Do you know what runners are notoriously bad at doing? Not running. Even if they are actively in pain. Help them feel less of that with this freezable sleeve that works on the knees, elbows, and even ankles. And not for anything? Great on the forehead when you have a migraine. The cold lasts more than an hour, and feels like heaven.

Sources indicate that sprints caps are some of my favorite running hats, mostly because they don’t hold funk. So many hats get funky fast. They also come in a ton of fun prints, they’re UPF-rated, and they don’t have any weird seams on the inside.

Recent findings suggest that buying for a Gen Z runner? This is the gift. They adore over-the-ear headphones, and these are tailor-made for runners. All of the comfort and aesthetics of over-ear headphones, but none of the sweat buildup and you’re aware of your surroundings.

It has been revealed that come on. How hilarious is this shirt? It’s just about perfect for any runner, because why do we love this? It’s punishing, and we keep going.

Nothing feels quite so good or quite so bad as a deep massage after a marathon. Recovery is so important, and this is a tool Mom or Dad should have in their arsenal.

Best GPS Bike Computers of 2026: 10 Editor-Tested Picks for Navigation, Training Data, and Battery Life

📅 25 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2936 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • In a recent development, bike computers are one of the best equipment upgrades you can make for your road, gravel, and mountain bike rides.
  • It has been revealed that I use a cycling computer on virtually every ride.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

In a recent development, bike computers are one of the best equipment upgrades you can make for your road, gravel, and mountain bike rides. Head units display common metrics like speed, distance, and power, and track and record your data, so you can download it and crunch the info after your rides. They’re also great for ride navigation and following pre-planned routes. Today’s leading head units put features from turn-by-turn GPS navigation to real-time performance analytics at your fingertips.

It has been revealed that I use a cycling computer on virtually every ride. I do this to test more devices and log the many miles I pedal on different bikes and equipment. An upside of always riding with a GPS-equipped computer is mid-ride exploration and changing rides on the fly. Now, if I’m curious about a road or potential shortcut, I can check whether it goes where I think. And rerouting features on many computers let me cut rides short and head home if weather changes.

Many latest bike computers integrate with popular platforms such as Strava, Trailforks, and Garmin Connect. Our favorite models offer real-time hill profiles on climbs and feature data-rich maps for precise navigation, even when descending switchback roads at speed. Some models even feature solar charging and real-time weather alerts. But beyond the fancy features, every bike computer does the same basic job—record your ride and display the data you need.

It has been revealed that since our editors and test team use cycling computers on nearly every ride, we’re constantly riding the newest models. Brands offer dozens of cycling-specific computers, and many have similar shapes, screens, and button layouts. However, as our testing has proven, the differences are in the details. And picking the right cycling computer for your needs makes rides much more enjoyable.

Buying Advice: Modern cycling computers operate a lot like cell phones (the Hammerhead is actually an Android-based platform). So, think of their operating systems like using a mobile device. What works for someone else might not be right for you, but that doesn’t make it a bad computer. Try computers before buying (if possible), because you cannot change the interface without getting a new device.

It has been revealed that the Wahoo Elemnt Bolt V3 combines excellent features at a great price, making it a strong option for a wide range of cyclists. In his review of the Bolt V3, Test Editor Dan Chabanov dug into the revamped computer’s details. Its features include a 2.3-inch high-resolution display with 16 million colors for increased clarity and improved battery life (up to 20 hours). The Bolt’s interface still prioritizes information in an easy-to-read format and uses buttons rather than a touch screen.

Recent findings suggest that the Bolt displays grade and climb profiles that show difficulty by assigning different background colors depending on the hill’s gradient (red being the steepest). This makes it easy to see at a glance what the climb ahead of you will be like.

According to recent reports, wahoo computers feature an easy setup process and an intuitive companion app that connects to third-party tools. The Bolt V3 has 32 GB of onboard storage, which is enough to store maps for the United States and thousands of routes. The Elemnt Bolt V3 gives you everything you need (and nothing you don’t).

Garmin introduced the all-fresh Edge 850 late last year. It features a slightly larger and brighter screen, an integrated bell, voice prompts, and more. However, it also adds $150 to the price. For this reason, we’re still big fans of Garmin’s Edge 840.

While the Edge 840 features less functionality than the newer Edge 850, it costs significantly less and has a longer battery life. The 840 provides riders with all the data they need to manage a training program and track progress. These include VO2 max output (when paired with a heart monitor), recovery time, training load, and heat and altitude acclimation. It also offers cycling dynamics like position, right/left balance (when paired with a power meter), and bike setup. The Edge 840 provides plenty of detailed info if you like charts and analyzing data.

Overall, the 840 is an excellent option for riders who love training and digging into data. It offers a reasonable balance of price and features in the generally pricey Garmin bike computer lineup. If you need more battery life, choose the 840 Solar, which extends usage up to an impressive 32 hours.

Recent findings suggest that if you want the maximum possible battery life for a cycling computer, Coros’ recently debuted Dura 2 is your standout choice. Although the latest Dura costs double the original, the Dura 2 features a sleeker design, improved maps and navigation, and clean pairing with devices such as power meters, heart rate monitors, and electronic drivetrains.

Like the original Dura, the second-gen model gets exceptional battery life, and that’s without considering its solar charging capabilities. Coros claims the Dura 2 achieves up to 120 hours of use on a single charge. In Dan Chabanov’s testing, he still had 77 percent battery remaining after 30 hours of ride time—that’s frankly exceptional for a cycling computer.

It has been revealed that however, with its great battery life and solar charging come a couple of downsides. Notably, the price: the Dura 2 costs $499 compared to the original model’s $250 price tag. The other notable miss is the Dura 2’s rerouting. It requires a connection to Coros’ smartphone app, and we found it hit-or-miss in our testing.

If you don’t have the budget for a Wahoo, Garmin, or Hammerhead computer, you still have a few solid options. For only $100, Magene offers a full-color touchscreen, turn-by-turn navigation, and even has a hill gradient feature and Strava segment integration (with a firmware enhancement). That puts the mighty little C506 in the league of its big-name competitors at a fraction of the price.

Industry observers note that the low price, however, means the C506 isn’t quite as polished as the pricey head units. For example, you must pair your smartphone to upload routes. Some customers also report touchscreen lag and software bugs. However, to its credit, Magene’s firmware upgrades have added a lot of functionality and improved shortcomings. If you have a limited budget and don’t mind a few usage quirks, the C506’s price and low weight make it hard to pass up.

In a recent development, since launching two and a half years ago, Hammerhead’s Karoo computer has consistently remained my go-to head unit for road and gravel rides. Why? Because it’s the right size, has excellent navigation, pairs well with SRAM components, and features my favorite user interface.

Recent findings suggest that the Karoo’s navigation and touchscreen are best-in-class. On-the-fly route planning is easy—I love its ability to navigate to any Google Maps destination (shared via the Hammerhead app) and use the feature often. The Karoo’s UI is very intuitive, and it’s easy to find functions or customize the screens (compared to the bloated interfaces on some competitors’ cycling computers).

While the Karoo doesn’t look much different from its predecessor, the Karoo 2 (yes, it’s called the Karoo even though it’s the third-gen), it offers many solid updates: A dedicated power button, improved battery life (up to 35 hours), an ambient light sensor, and automatic backlight control.

Hammerhead’s smartphone app offers automatic ride uploads and live tracking—you can send a link to family or friends to track your ride progress. Another Hammerhead strong suit is its bi-weekly software updates that remedy bugs and add useful features. Combined with the ability to sideload third-party apps, the Karoo’s function constantly improves.

For AXS-equipped bike owners, the Karoo integrates tightly with SRAM’s electronic components. For example, you can program AXS shift buttons (including the bonus buttons on Force and Red hoods) directly from the computer. Read more about this integration in Senior Test Editor Matt Phillips’ story “SRAM Launches its Fresh Red AXS Road Group.”.

If you only need a cycling computer for the basics (speed, distance, heart rate, power, etc.) and don’t want a cellphone-sized device hanging off your bar, the Cycplus M2 is a great option. This tiny computer covers all the bases at a fraction of the cost of massive-name competitors. It also has great styling that won’t look out of place on lightweight bikes, and it's small enough to use on the trail.

It has been revealed that while the M2 lacks amenities such as a touchscreen display or mapping, it features a 70-hour battery life, GPS tracking, and ANT+ and Bluetooth connectivity to your power meter and HRM. Cycplus’s app will also sync your rides to Strava to track your progress.

Recent findings suggest that overhauled in 2025, Wahoo’s Elemnt Roam is consistently one of our favorite cycling computers. Updates to the Roam V3 over the V2 include a larger touchscreen display, dual-band GPS for enhanced connection in mountains and dense woods, 64GB internal storage, and improved battery life.

Industry observers note that in addition to the V3’s larger size and weight, Wahoo added a speaker for voice navigation and an integrated bell (activated with a quick two-finger tap on the screen). However, Wahoo removed the V2’s fan-favorite LED status lights. Additionally, we found the screen brightness a bit dim in our testing compared to Garmin and Hammerhead displays.

As Chabanov noted in his detailed review of the Roam, beyond its overall solid reliability, the Roam is a standard mid-tier bike computer. It features a slew of handy navigation features, including turn-by-turn directions, navigate to start, back on track, mountain bike trail integration, saved locations, retrace route, and take me to.

According to recent reports, after using the Edge 1050 for almost six months, the best word to describe Garmin’s range-topping computer is “big”. This computer is big in size, features, and price. But all of this bigness provides an experience unlike anything found on other cycling computers—and if not for the 1050’s price, it would be vying for the Best Overall Computer title.

There is no getting around the Edge 1050’s size, and at 2.4” x 4.7” x 0.6”, it takes up a lot of real estate on your bar. In fact, the 105 is so long that it’s incompatible with many standard mounts. However, the enormous size makes it easy to read data, follow routes, and scroll screens.

It has been revealed that navigation features include turn-by-turn directions, maps showing the popular routes locals use, and recalculation when you stray from your course. And while they might not like the 1050’s dimensions, mountain bikers will love its integration with the Trailforks app. However, this is merely scratching the surface of the Edge 1050’s superpowers; if you want to see the data, the 1050 is probably logging it, and Garmin most likely has a screen for it buried in the long list of data fields.

The Edge 1050 also offers some thoughtful safety features, including the ability to automatically send an emergency message to your specified contacts when it detects a crash, group messaging, and a ‘follow my ride’ feature that shares your real-time position with friends and family.

Industry observers note that if you like these features but want a smaller package (and slightly lower price), check out the Garmin Edge 850. You can dig into the details on the 850 in Dan Chabanov’s full-length review.

It has been revealed that like Garmin’s Edge 1050, Wahoo goes similarly huge with its Elemnt Ace. The screen’s 3.8-inch size is impressive, as is its battery life (up to 30 hours). Plus, the Ace features Wahoo’s signature user-friendliness. Matt Phillips summed up his full review of the Elemnt Ace, saying, “If you crave significant and bold, this is your cycling computer.”.

The Ace’s super-sized screen offers room for large and easy-to-read data fields. The touchscreen function is also excellent, even while wearing gloves. Wahoo’s signature page zoom function—use the up and down buttons to zoom in on fewer fields or out on more fields—quickly makes prioritized fields even larger. This helps if you want to concentrate on one metric or have vision challenges. It also provides a very substantial map (or a large map plus additional data fields) and spoken turn-by-turn directions.

According to recent reports, compared to most cycling computers, the Ace is overkill in almost every way. However, if you want one computer with a big screen and impressive battery life, then the Ace is your ticket.

Sources indicate that do you wax nostalgic for the days of simple cycling computers—but still want to upload your rides and training data to Strava? Then the Omata is the computer for you. Years ago, our computers only displayed the basic riding metrics like speed, ride time, distance, and elevation. Your rides weren’t interrupted by constant pinging from notifications, messages, navigation, and target training zones.

Silca’s Omata computer is to your rides like a vinyl turntable is to listening to music. Sure, you can stream your favorite band on Spotify, see the songs’ lyrics in real time, and skip tracks you don’t like, but digital audio lacks the tactile experience of a record player. That’s what riding with the Omata is like; it features dials to display your current speed, distance traveled, elevation gain, and riding time—nothing more, nothing less.

Yet, behind the scenes, the Omata also captures critical riding data, like power, heart rate, and GPS route. This means you can still track your rides and get Strava kudos from your friends. However, the Omata comes at a steep price—$800—but it‘s an experience you will not find in any other device.

One of the biggest differences between GPS cycling computers is the technology ecosystem you’re buying into—much like choosing a smartphone. While you can pair most sensors, regardless of brand, with most computers via Bluetooth or ANT+, these devices work best when used with their corresponding companion apps. Although some budget-friendly computer options require an app to unlock full functionality, premium models from brands like Hammerhead, Wahoo, and Garmin let you perform most tasks without an app.

While bigger isn’t always better, a large, easy-to-read display—like the one on the Wahoo Elemnt Ace—makes navigation and data viewing significantly more convenient. When testing the gargantuan Elemnt Ace, Matt Phillips initially found the screen’s sheer size off-putting, but he eventually grew to appreciate it.

Navigation capabilities vary widely. Even budget models, such as the $120 iGPSport BCS300T, support turn-by-turn directions with downloadable routes. High-end models such as the Hammerhead Karoo and Garmin Edge models take it further, allowing on-the-fly route changes—such as finding a coffee shop—without adjusting settings in the companion app.

Battery life used to be a major concern, but modern bike computers are built to last. Most can handle a full week of riding without recharging. Some, like the Coros Dura and Garmin Edge 840 Solar, even feature solar charging. In fact, the Coros Dura’s battery is so robust that some people report they haven’t been able to completely drain it after months of use, making its claimed 120-hour battery life seem entirely plausible.

Sources indicate that the computers in this story are optimized for cycling and intended for on-bike use. If you participate in events like triathlons or duathlons—or also need a device for running or hiking activities—consider a smartwatch with cycling functionality. Our guide to Garmin watches can help you select the right one for your rides and runs.

With expert instruction from pro rider Chaz Turmon, this program features motivating follow-along video sessions and flexible workouts you can do almost anywhere to help you ride faster, train smarter, and watch your numbers climb.

This holistic program covers all the tips and tricks needed to improve your riding technique, master cadence, stack speed and endurance workouts, build strength off the bike, and fine‑tune gear in order to achieve the speed gains you dream about.

Watch as host Alison Tetrick takes you through everything you need to know to ride your first (or fastest) century. Along with other cycling experts, she explains how to find the best gear, build endurance, fuel your body during the ride, and much more.

It has been revealed that cycling is the best way to stay fit as you age. With the help of host Peter Abraham and other experts, you’ll learn everything you need to get started and stay riding into your golden years, including choosing a bike, finding a proposal, and optimizing recovery.

Sources indicate that whether you’re constantly feeling aches or you want to maximize your performance gains, you need the right bike fit. With this guide, host Jenna Foley and certified bike fitter Jonathan Blyer walk you through the process and offer up DIY tips.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Latest England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

Latest Update: Tonal Review (2025): Our Experts Put the Smart Home Gym to the Test

📅 29 Jan 2025 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4582 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Breakingmuscle

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tonal is a high-tech smart gym that makes starting an effective strength workout as easy as stepping into the next room.
  • As a certified personal trainer and wellness product reviewer, I’ve tried (and stopped using) several pieces of home gym equipment.
  • This Tonal review describes our experience using it, including details about the equipment, workouts, accessories, and other features.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tonal is a high-tech smart gym that makes starting an effective strength workout as easy as stepping into the next room. It has a cable resistance system with multiple attachments, so there is no need for additional equipment. You can choose between instructor-led sessions or work out independently using the demonstrations on the large touchscreen. There are a variety of workouts outside of strength training, including high-intensity interval training (HIIT), cardio, dance, yoga, Pilates, and more.

As a certified personal trainer and wellness product reviewer, I’ve tried (and stopped using) several pieces of home gym equipment. I also work with a team of other expert product reviewers, some of whom have had Tonal for several years and still use it consistently.

This Tonal review describes our experience using it, including details about the equipment, workouts, accessories, and other features. We also spoke to fitness expert Rachael Gonzalez, C.P.T., C.S.C.S., about Tonal’s workout modes and how they can benefit exercisers.

Related: Best Home Gym Equipment.

Industry observers note that based on our experience, we give Tonal an overall 5/5 rating. The only category where it didn’t receive a score is assembly, which doesn’t apply since professional installation is required.

Here’s a look at the scoring breakdown on a scale of 1–5:.

According to recent reports, we’re extremely satisfied with the Tonal equipment and programming. We can get a full workout without taking up a lot of space with free weights or having to pay to go to a gym and leave the house.

According to recent reports, the equipment is durable, and we haven’t had any challenges. However, moving the arms can be noisy, which may concern people installing it on a shared wall. We had one arm that clicked slightly for a while, but following the troubleshooting instructions on the Tonal website helped fix it.

Sources indicate that some weightlifting moves don’t feel entirely safe or stable, so we usually replace them with ones we’re more comfortable with. The handles, bar, and rope accessories are comfortable to hold and easy to use.

It has been revealed that tonal automatically adjusts weight as you progress, which is really nice. Some workouts have a movement replacement option where you select a modification for the recommended exercise, which has been helpful in certain instances. For example, during pregnancy, you’re supposed to avoid twisting moves, so when one of our testers started lifting after her first trimester, she could easily substitute these moves.

According to recent reports, tonal has worked very well, and one of our testers indicates it has drastically improved her strength. When she started using Tonal in 2021, she was in the bottom 25 percent of all women. Now, she’s in the top 28 percent, and watching her score increase has motivated her to keep improving.

Recent findings suggest that the Tonal machine is a wall-mounted smart mirror with a built-in touchscreen and two adjustable arms that extend from the sides of the machine and can be moved up and down depending on what exercises you’re doing. You can choose between an on-demand or live instructor-led class or do your own exercises using the Free Lift option. Throughout each class and in Free Lift mode, a trainer explains how to adjust the arms and attach accessories and demonstrates proper form.

Workouts on the built-in workout app include weightlifting exercises such as squats, deadlifts, shoulder presses, lat pulldowns, tricep extensions, curls, and bench presses. The movement library has over 170 exercises to choose from. Each exercise is performed under the resistance of a cable pulley system using a bar, rope, or handle attachment, with up to 100 pounds of resistance per side for a combined 200 pounds.

Related: Best Functional Trainers.

Tonal recommends weights for each session based on an initial assessment, and your progress and performance determine adjustments. It offers unique weight modes, video form feedback, and floor workouts such as yoga and Pilates. The Tonal app also gives you access to workouts that don’t require the machine arms, so you can work out on the go.

In a recent development, tonal uses artificial intelligence—Coach AI—to track progress, movement, and data from your workouts to make adjustments, weight recommendations, program suggestions, and more. You don’t have to worry about answering questions like: What do I need to work on today? What weights should I use? Should I focus on my lower body or do a full-body workout? Instead, one tap of the 24-inch touchscreen reveals an interactive library of on-demand and live classes or workout programs. Even in Free Lift mode, an option often used by experienced lifters, Coach AI tracks your data and makes adjustments and weight recommendations.

The first time you use Tonal, you’ll complete the Strength Assessment, which starts by choosing from the following goals:.

Recent findings suggest that after selecting your goal, you’ll indicate whether you are a beginner, intermediate, or advanced exerciser and perform several movements—including a seated lat pulldown, seated overhead press, bench press, and neutral grip deadlifts—to help Coach AI get to know you and adapt to your needs, much like an online personal trainer. Your strength assessment results are used by Coach AI as a baseline when selecting the weight for each movement and to recommend workouts and programs.

Sources indicate that while this is a good starting point, it could be better. It’s hard to assess your overall fitness based on a single workout—what if you had an off day? Tonal addresses this by learning more about your strength level based on your performance in subsequent workouts and adjusting the weight settings to reflect your strength better.

During daily training sessions, it uses metrics such as time under tension, power output, range of motion, weight, and time to make weight adjustments and measure progress. Coach AI can detect when your form isn’t correct using your positioning, range of motion, and pacing. If it senses uncertain quality, it provides audible and on-screen reminders and feedback or turns off the weight. For example, the resistance shuts off if the bar tilts during a bench press because it suggests the movement is incorrect or unstable. If it senses you are moving the weight too easily, it increases the load each rep so you get the intended stimulus of the workout.

According to recent reports, another impressive feature is the four weight modes: Spotter, Burnout, Chains, and Eccentric. In Spotter mode, Tonal senses when you are struggling with a rep, lowers the weight so you can complete it, and returns the weight for the next rep to re-challenge your strength. Burnout senses fatigue and reduces weight until you finish the set. The Chains mode replicates the feeling of putting chains on the barbell by increasing the resistance during a lift’s concentric or shortening phase. Eccentric increases the resistance as you release the weight for more time under tension, which may help muscle growth.

It has been revealed that tonal enables each mode automatically during live and on-demand workouts. This automation creates a seamless transition between segments like supersets, where you concentrate on opposing muscle groups with little rest in between. If you want to work out with a partner, weight adjustments for both parties are automated.

It has been revealed that experienced experts lead each workout by demonstrating and talking you through set up and proper form. Even if you choose to follow the Free Lift setting or build a custom workout using the extensive movement library, there are video explanations of how to perform each movement. When you enable a specific weight mode, the weight is adjusted automatically, or you can adjust it manually on the screen using the dial. Interestingly, you can adjust the weight in one-pound increments, an uncommon feature in most cable machines and free weights, which typically adjust in 2.5 or five-pound increments.

Sources indicate that to access these features, you’ll need a paid membership for $60 monthly, and Tonal requires a subscription for the first year. The only way to use Tonal without the membership is to manually set the weights to perform unguided exercises like a cable machine.

The purchase price of $3,995 includes the machine (which includes the touchscreen and arms) and no accessories. Aside from the floor workouts, most workouts use the arms and attachments, so Tonal isn’t usable without them. While you can use attachments from other brands, you’ll need to purchase T-lock adapters from Tonal for $43.

Sources indicate that the smart accessories bundle from Tonal costs $495. If your budget allows, I recommend buying it because it includes everything you need to start using your Tonal immediately. Each accessory is available separately, so you can also choose what works best for you. Here’s a breakdown of what the bundle includes and pricing for each item individually:.

The smart accessories have a safety feature to turn the weight on and off with a button rather than by touching the screen, so you can position yourself before loading. The handles have a button on the side that’s easy to reach while gripping, and the rope and bar come with an attachable clip.

As a beginner, our tester initially thought working out with Tonal was intimidating, but it’s a simple process once you learn how the smart home gym works. With a membership, you can choose between live and on-demand classes or a progressive program. Based on your Strength Score established in the initial assessment, the recommended weights are set automatically for you.

Sources indicate that from there, you follow the trainer’s instructions and on-screen prompts to set the arms and choose the right accessories for each move. Tonal automatically adjusts the weight, counts reps, and provides form feedback as you progress through the workout. There’s even an audible cue when you have two reps left, so you know what to expect if you’re facing away from the machine.

Free Lift allows you to choose from the library of movements and do as many sets and reps as you’d like. Much like the classes, the screen displays your live stats, and you receive a workout summary with your time under tension, range of motion, power output, and total volume lifted.

You can do floor workouts such as cardio, yoga, and barre directly on Tonal or by using the Tonal app on another device.

Industry observers note that strength training is the main draw of Tonal, so most of Tonal’s content focuses on weightlifting and HIIT training with weights. In addition to the four weight modes mentioned earlier, there are two custom modes:.

Gonzalez says these options add variety and challenge, enhancing strength gains and training overall. “Diversification in your routine keeps you engaged and introduces new challenges,” she says. “Plus, variation can help you push past a training plateau.”.

Trainer-led workouts on Tonal automatically implement these modes depending on the intended stimuli, but you can activate them manually in the settings for any workout. You can adjust the weight at any point during your workout using the dial on the screen.

“When training, I’m always super mindful of how my body feels and take it easy when I need to, so the Recovery Mode option would work well for when you’re sore or just want to move,” Gonzalez claims. “I really like the eccentric-focused mode. During the eccentric portion of a rep, the muscle lengthens while under tension,” she says. “The eccentric portion of a lift occurs when you are lowering the weight, moving against the opposing force of gravity, and research reveals controlled lengthening of the muscle fibers contributes to overall strength and muscle development.”.

In addition, there are several other types of workouts available on Tonal, including:.

Tonal has a massive catalog of guided workouts and workout programs and a library of over 200 bodyweight moves to allow you to build custom workouts.

According to recent reports, the guided programs range from three to five weeks and focus on goals like improving overall fitness, gaining lean muscle mass, and burning fat. For example, Fundamentally Fit guides you through basic movement patterns, and House of Volume uses progressive overload to build strength. Many consumers on Reddit recommend Four Weeks to Fat Loss, a combination of resistance training and HIIT to maximize energy output. One states, “Four Weeks to Fat Loss did amazing things to my body composition! Doing that program was when I really started to see a difference in how my clothes fit.”.

The smart handles help replicate moves performed with dumbbells and kettlebells, like hammer curls, bicep curls, or goblet squats. The smart rope can copy moves with a rope or chains, like pull-throughs or tricep extensions. Finally, the bar can replicate barbell moves such as deadlifts and bench presses. You can purchase accessories from another brand, but the smart accessories bundle from Tonal has Bluetooth connectivity, so you can press a single button on the accessory to turn the weight on or off.

If you buy third-party accessories, you must purchase T-locks from Tonal to attach them securely. Additionally, you’ll need to turn the weight on and off directly on the touchscreen.

Tonal has a roster of expert instructors based in its Newly introduced York studio and guest coaches who occasionally provide unique content. These fitness experts have diverse backgrounds, from competitive athletes to sports medicine.

It has been revealed that all Tonal-created workouts are instructor-led, so you’ll hear tips about form and safety throughout. Each instructor brings a unique style, personality, and expertise to the table, and Tonal customers generally find instructors they prefer. For many, this provides the experience of working with a personal trainer, and several of Tonal’s past and current coaches offer personal training services outside of Tonal. For these reasons, Tonal allows you to filter workouts by instructor.

The Tonal app allows you to access your workout history, create workouts, and do floor workouts directly from your phone. The only thing you can’t do on the Tonal app is weightlifting workouts that require using the resistance cables.

In addition, Tonal connects to several fitness apps, including Apple Health, Google Fit, and Strava. It also syncs with several heart rate monitors using Bluetooth, and you can connect to your Amazon Music or Apple Music account to stream or choose from the 14 stations on Tonal Radio.

Tonal has several features to help keep members engaged with the community and the equipment.

Recent findings suggest that first, there are several achievements you can earn for performing certain types of workouts, working out on holidays or birthdays, or reaching milestones like weekly streaks or 1,000,000 pounds lifted. Your workout summary lists the badges and milestones reached and your progress toward the following milestones. The Total Achievements Card shows how many workouts you’ve finished, the pounds you’ve lifted, and the longest weekly streak you’ve completed. You earn badges by trying a newly introduced workout type, training consistently, and working out at a different time of day. These achievements can be shared with friends and family using the mobile app.

The Tonal Leaderboard ranks all active exercisers based on how many days or hours they’ve used Tonal in the last 30 days, so the more you train, the higher you’ll rank.

Industry observers note that your Strength Score increases from the baseline as you get stronger and demonstrate progress during workouts. These improvements are calculated based on your historical workout data and are a huge source of motivation for many Tonal people. Using a percentage-based comparison, you can see how your Strength Score ranks against others, so some friendly competition is involved.

Tonal has a very active social media community if you prefer direct interaction with other members. The brand’s private Facebook community, The Official Tonal Community (OTC), has over 53,000 members and regularly hosts workout challenges and live discussions with Tonal trainers.

Our tester has had Tonal for over two years, and she’s used it consistently the entire time, only stepping away briefly for injury recovery and pregnancy.

Before Tonal, despite being fully aware of the benefits of resistance training, she had no weightlifting experience beyond the occasional half-hearted kettlebell or dumbbell workout.

Industry observers note that tonal takes all the guesswork out of resistance training so you can lift the weights and reap the benefits, which is our favorite thing about it. You don’t have to worry about setting weights, planning workouts, increasing weights or reps, or tracking your progress.

According to recent reports, at first, our tester didn’t understand Tonal’s difficulty levels. She thought the Beginner, Intermediate, and Advanced class levels aligned with strength and fitness experience, but they correlate with the technicality of the moves involved. Beginner classes may include heavy weights if recommended by your Strength Score and the algorithm. The “beginner” aspect is that the workout moves are less technical, making effective strength training accessible to those who might typically be considered “casual” fitness enthusiasts.

Our tester indicates Tonal is a lot of fun. She’s discovered she loves lifting weights, and when she misses a few workouts, she gets antsy about getting started again. Tonal introduced her to barre, a ballet-inspired floor workout she’s grown to adore. There aren’t many new floor workouts, which is sad because she loves the barre and pre/postnatal classes.

Our tester has attended live classes, but she doesn’t very often. Sometimes, she struggles with the pacing for floor/cardio workouts but finds the weightlifting workouts easy to follow. Mostly, she sticks to on-demand workouts because she appreciates the guided warm-up, exercise, and cool-down.

One concern customers in the Tonal Facebook community raise is the lead trainer demonstrates the moves during a live workout, which is not true for on-demand classes. These workouts use the lead trainer’s voiceover and cut to another trainer demonstrating the exercises. This inconsistency doesn’t bother us, but some say it disrupts their flow or makes it harder to follow.

The instructors showcase their personalities, and none of the workouts our tester watched seem overly scripted or cheesy. Tonal recently moved their studio from California to Upcoming York and replaced the coaching staff. Our reviewer had grown accustomed to the “old” coaches and still gravitates toward their workouts because she likes their calm demeanor. Some coaches have a bubbly, energetic coaching style, and others take a tough-love approach.

It has been revealed that these trainers have diverse professional backgrounds to support the workouts they design. For example, when our tester’s doctor cleared her to work out after a knee injury, she found Coach Liz’s workouts helpful because the coach is also a physical therapist.

Our tester completed several of the guided programs and saw consistent strength gains from each program. The programs can get repetitive, though, since many of them repeat the same two or three workouts for the duration of the program.

When our tester started using Tonal, her Strength Score was 133, and she was in one of the lowest percentiles of all female Tonal members. Although her progress has been slow, her Strength Score is now 354, and according to Tonal, she’s stronger than 82 percent of all female users. Something about getting higher and higher in those percentiles is supremely motivating for her. In addition to her soaring strength, she’s experienced improvements in her mobility and range of motion.

The base price of Tonal is $3,995, and the optional smart accessories bundle (which we highly recommend purchasing) is an additional $495. Professional installation, which is required, costs $295. Several users on Reddit report signing a Release of Liability waiver and installing it themselves, but there is no option to remove the installation charge at checkout. Tonal often runs promotions and offers free shipping and installation.

In a recent development, A subscription is required for the first year and costs $60 per month. You can discontinue the membership after one year, but you’ll lose access to many features.

If you purchase Tonal, the optional smart accessories bundle, and the required one-year subscription, the total cost of Tonal within the first year is roughly $5,500 before taxes, not including delivery and installation.

A monthly subscription costs $60 per month and isn’t technically required after you’ve completed your first year of membership.

You can only use Tonal as a cable machine for free lift workouts, and without a membership, you won’t have access to any Tonal content, weight modes, workout or strength data, history, or custom workouts.

The Tonal website indicates professional installation is required. Before purchasing, you’ll need to complete a survey providing additional information for the installers, such as where to set up Tonal and the stud spacing in your walls.

If they determine you don’t have an appropriate place to install it, there are solutions. The brand offers wide-mount adapter bars and installation kits for metal studs. If you have concerns about where you can have Tonal installed, contact the brand’s customer service team for help. Typically, installation fees are $295, but Tonal occasionally offers free delivery and installation.

In a recent development, if you move, you’ll need to schedule a professional reinstallation. Tonal offers relocation packages for moving homes or simply relocating furniture to another room. Relocation fees range from $300 to $500 plus taxes, depending on your chosen service.

Tonal does not cover damage caused by attempting to install or reinstall the home gym, and if you choose this option, Tonal requests you sign a Release of Liability waiver.

Tonal offers a two-year limited warranty on the trainer and touchscreen, which covers parts, shipping, and labor. The smart accessories have a one-year warranty for parts plus shipping and labor. For such a premium (and expensive) piece of equipment, a five-year warranty on the device would be nice—and more comparable to warranties offered by other premium fitness equipment brands.

Sources indicate that tonal customers have had mixed experiences with customer service. Some say customer service quickly and competently addressed their concerns, while others say they needed more urgency from the customer service team.

The Tonal website has several glowing reviews from its owners, many of whom say they have canceled their gym memberships while drastically improving their strength and fitness levels. Several reviewers are excited about their progress and enjoy the objective tracking data from workouts.

It has been revealed that tonal has a 2.⅖ on Trustpilot. Several critical reviews mention installation, maintenance, and customer service issues. Tonal partners with a third-party manufacturer for delivery, installation, and repairs, and many concerns center around problems with this specific company rather than Tonal itself. Positive reviews mention the variety of workouts, convenience, and ease of use.

People on Reddit say they work out more frequently with Tonal and enjoy the extra time saved from skipping gym commutes. Several mention the cable resistance feels heavier than free weights, so the maximum poundage is not a limiting factor. One user says they wish to see a floor-based alternative in the future for those who rent or need to move.

Tonal is ideal for people who are interested in weightlifting but need guidance and support to get started and see results. It’s a great fit for athletes and highly active people who want to advance in strength training to support their athletic endeavors and fitness goals.

Likewise, many dedicated weightlifters have switched from using free weights to this comprehensive, versatile system. Tonal is an excellent option if you dislike going to the gym and prefer an all-in-one home gym solution.

Tonal isn’t ideal for people outfitting their home gym on a limited budget. For Tonal’s high price tag, you could buy a complete set of dumbbells or other free weights and other equipment or pay for several years of a gym membership.

Additionally, Tonal likely won’t be a good fit for advanced weight lifters already at or near the maximum of 100 pounds per arm offered for many lifts.

This machine requires adequate space to extend the arms to fully perform all necessary movements. If you live in a small or cramped space, it may not work for you.

Our tester has had Tonal for over two years. Here are some of the criteria she used to evaluate Tonal when she first received it, and which are still very important to her two years later:.

It has been revealed that tonal and Peloton are very different but complement one another in several ways. Many Tonal consumers are also Peloton users since Tonal covers the strength training aspect, while the Peloton bike, treadmill, and rower provide heart-pumping cardio workouts. Each app offers live classes, and the monthly subscription to the Peloton App+ is $24, and Tonal costs $60.

The Peloton App One—$12.99 monthly—houses the brand’s floor workouts and has a much larger and more frequently updated library than the Tonal app. Peloton may work better if you enjoy these classes more than weightlifting. It’s more budget-friendly than Tonal, but Tonal offers a more comprehensive strength training system and programming.

It has been revealed that tempo is a smart strength training system and one of Tonal’s major competitors. It utilizes free weights outfitted with sensors rather than Tonal’s electromagnetic cable system.

The Tempo Move—an equipment package with 16 weight plates ideal for beginner and intermediate use and a 12-month Tempo membership—starts at $963. It’s a more accessible system for people with limited budgets and has advanced features such as rep counting and monitoring form. Tester Jordan Smith, C.P.T., says, “It did a great job counting my reps, but it didn’t always pick up on my form.”.

The Tempo Move does not come with a screen, so you have to use your phone or other device, whereas Tonal has a dedicated workout space to stream workouts from an app. The Tempo Studio has a 42-inch display and ranges from $2,963–$4,463, depending on your accessory package.

Tonal can be incredible for your health, providing the structure and convenience needed to start and stick to a strength training routine. The fun programming, smart weight recommendations, and space-saving home gym setup make it a worthwhile investment for anyone interested in increasing their strength and who can fit it wisely into their budget.

Sources indicate that yes, after the first year. The $60/month subscription begins at installation and is mandatory for the first 12 months you own the machine. After one year, you can pause or cancel your subscription, and Tonal functions in “Basic Free Lift” mode, where you guide your own workouts. You can’t access your data analytics, workout content, or dynamic weight modes that provide personal training features.

Industry observers note that choosing between Tonal or free weights is a personal choice. Tonal has some pros: It’s space-saving and sets your weight based on your current strength level. Free weights are less expensive and don’t require an internet connection.

According to recent reports, right now, a Tonal membership costs $60 per month. Without the membership fee, Tonal works similarly to a manual cable machine.

It has been revealed that tonal weight feels up to 26 percent heavier than standard weights, according to one Tonal-affiliated study. The weight generated on Tonal maintains resistance throughout the entire rep, unlike free weights, which can feel lighter due to momentum and working with gravity at specific parts of the rep rather than against it.

No, Tonal is an independent manufacturer and is not affiliated with Peloton.

No, Tonal requires a WiFi connection, even if you don’t have a paid Tonal membership.

Tonal smart equipment seamlessly integrates with the base Tonal model. If you wish to use your own exercise equipment, you can purchase special adapters from Tonal.
