Recent findings suggest that the fund returned -7%Â¹, giving back much of last quarter's gains. Thus we are still digging out of our hole. Returns will differ by fund; please check your individual statements.

Most of what you will read in this letter comes down to one idea: the market has gotten worse at seeing. Michael Mauboussin and Dan Callahan of Morgan Stanley estimate that fundamental investors now account for only about 15% of trading volume, with much of the rest driven by quant funds and high-frequency traders. These strategies differ, but many rely on readily measurable inputs such as earnings estimates and price momentum. The information we care about often sits outside the view of many participants: in 1,000-page insurance filings, press releases that never name the customer, or hard-to-access court filings.

Industry observers note that human investors are increasingly using large language models such as ChatGPT and Claude as their first research stop. These tools allow us to cover ground quickly, but they can also reinforce consensus. When many investors ask similar questions and start with summaries of what has already been written about a company, they are likely to encounter similar explanations for what matters and what comes next. This leaves fewer investors examining the "other side of the trade." If that is happening, changes in consensus could produce more pronounced movesâa pattern consistent with my market observations.

Recent findings suggest that our portfolio is full of companies where I believe value is accruing outside the market's current focus. These dynamics may help explain why the gap between business performance and share price this year has been so wide. For several of our largest holdings, there are specific milestones over the coming quarters that should make their progress visible even to the computers, whether through reported earnings, settlements, or a sale. This letter walks through those milestones, company by company.

In a recent development, in the last letter, I wrote that I believed that many of our holdings were non-consensus but right, which Howard Marks and others have pointed out is the quadrant that generates the most attractive returns. At the very end of the letter, I condensed it to the following checklist:.

- Lifecore (LFCR). The strategic process results in a sale or another outcome that closes the valuation gap.

- AnaptysBio. GSK (GSK) resolves the dispute through a settlement or acquisition.

- Burford. The protein cases produce large settlements as they move through summary judgment.

Sources indicate that - Kingsway (KFS). Double-digit organic growth, accelerating EBITDA, and additional acquisitions.

- Hagerty (HGTY). Operating leverage returns and results beat consensus estimates.

It has been revealed that - Cellebrite (CLBT). Genesis generates meaningful revenue and Cellebrite begins to be viewed as an AI beneficiary.

Recent findings suggest that - Compass Diversified (CODI). Assets are sold, shares are repurchased, and management is internalized.

Because the catalysts are idiosyncratic and each has its own timeline, I want to structure this letter primarily as an update on these companies and how each thesis is tracking.

It has been revealed that where appropriate, I will highlight areas where it is difficult for the âmarketâ to see what is going on and how our thesis can be non-consensus and right. Seeing something before the computers only matters if there is a path to it showing up in the financials and the stock can ârerateâ as the computers see what we see.

Lifecore took a very large step toward realizing our thesis that âthe strategic process results in a sale or another outcome that closes the valuation gap.â On September 28, Lifecore confirmed an agreement to be acquired at a nearly 50% premium to where the shares traded just before the announcement.

According to recent reports, in the weeks before the offer, I spent a lot of time re-underwriting Lifecore. The tech giant was executing operationally and winning fresh business, yet the share price kept drifting down. The divergence was so great (in my opinion) that I wanted to question everything.

It has been revealed that part of the problem is that progress is hard to see. The FDA approval process takes roughly two years, so a customer win today will likely start showing up in revenue at the end of 2028 and in earnest in 2029 as production ramps. If you look in Bloomberg for consensus 2028 or 2029 revenue or earnings numbers for Lifecore, you wonât find any. It is as if the customer wins do not exist in forward projections on Bloomberg.

Industry observers note that it is also hard to infer progress from disclosures. Lifecoreâs customers do not want the manufacturer to announce their names, the drugs being manufactured, or expected volumes. As the graphic below demonstrates, Lifecore has won at least 18 programs, most declared via press release or on an earnings call, none naming the customer or contract size.

It has been revealed that the announcements do contain clues. The language is carefully chosen. A âcommercial transferâ means Lifecore is taking over manufacturing of a drug that is already approved and on the market with proven demand. Commercial transfers move faster and are more likely to become revenue. New drugs and Phase III programs are more speculative. They take longer than 24 months and still need FDA approval.

Some announcements also hint at size: âa potential top-5 customer, â â5% to 10% of capacity, â or âan eight-figure opportunity.â Together they build the foundation for a view on 2028 and 2029 even if the analysts wonât provide one.

Below is a partial example, estimating the size and probability of success of selected programs listed above.Â².

Sources indicate that laid out visually, the same exercise reveals how effective new management has been at selling excess capacity. We can lament the share price, but CEO Paul Josephs inherited a broken sales organization that is now working.

It has been revealed that each commercial agreement on the date it was declared. Bubble area = estimated peak annual revenue (firm tiers); color = our conversion odds.

I have attached a longer presentation with the full build for 2028 and 2029. It was very helpful in holding the position when Mr. Market had clearly given up. My bottom-up build has revenue and EBITDA compounding at 21% and 34%, respectively, and if the sales cadence continues, there is a path to a revenue CAGR above 30% and an EBITDA CAGR above 40% through 2029. Applying what I believe is a reasonable low-double-digit EBITDA multiple for a fast-growing business with extremely sticky customers, operating leverage, and contracted growth gets me to a double-digit share price.

The current offer is $6.28 per share plus additional consideration if the manufacturer hits certain milestones in 2028 through 2030. I have remarked repeatedly that I think the company is worth more than $10 per share, but even in the best-case scenario, if it hits all of the milestones, total deal consideration would be $9.67. I think there are a couple of factors at play.

One of Lifecoreâs largest shareholders is a fund run by a board member, and its most recent 13F highlights the fund down to two holdings, which suggests it is winding down. That may have accelerated the sale process. In addition, the low share price is an impediment to a high offer as buyers typically don't offer a premium of more than 100% to the current share price unless there are intense competitive dynamics at play or an unwilling seller.

It has been revealed that I don't think the offer reflects fair value and we are evaluating how to vote. The deal leaves room for a superior offer. The deal is structured with a small breakup fee of $7M for a superior offer during the 30-day go-shop period and $9M for the period after the go-shop ends and before the deal closes. The deal is anticipated to close in the fourth quarter. We will see over the next two months whether another buyer agrees with our assessment and submits a higher offer.

It has been revealed that the shortest update belongs to AnaptysBio (ANAB), which is suing the much larger GSK. As a reminder, AnaptysBio discovered the cancer drug Jemperli and licensed it to Tesaro, which GSK bought in 2019. Part of the deal was a promise not to run cancer trials with competing drugs of the same type, and AnaptysBio claims GSK broke that promise. The restriction makes less and less sense for GSK as it spends billions building out its cancer business.

Industry observers note that GSK has tried to buy AnaptysBio multiple times. I expect GSK to either buy AnaptysBio outright or revise the royalty agreement before a final ruling, allowing GSK to gain full control of its cancer program for a fraction of what it has invested. Given the facts of the case and AnaptysBio's strong underlying economics, a 50%+ premium to our purchase price is well within my range of potential outcomes. The post-trial hearing was October 20, with a ruling expected in Q1 or Q2 2027, so we will see soon if GSK tries to buy AnaptysBio again.

According to recent reports, earnings estimates, one of the largest inputs for quants, are largely irrelevant here. The thesis rests on GSK's incentive to buy, and seeing that takes more than a Google search. I may be right or wrong, but I am almost certainly playing outside the view of many market participants.

Our other "legal" investment is Burford Capital (BUR). Last quarter I wrote that being right would mean "the protein cases produce large settlements as they move through summary judgment." Here is where that stands.

It has been revealed that there are four protein cases: chicken, pork, beef, and turkey. Chicken is the largest and furthest along; what remain are the "opt-outs, " buyers who left the class-action suits because they expect to do better on their own. By our count, 23 groups of opt-outs have unresolved claims against Pilgrim's and 33 against Tyson.

Recent findings suggest that burford holds the largest unsettled claims against Pilgrim's Pride (PPC) and the second largest against Tyson. Neither company can put chicken behind it without going to trial or settling with Burford. Both have made large payments to other opt-outs to avoid going to trial. Since 2020, Tyson has paid or reserved about $800M for chicken claims and Pilgrim's has recorded about $1.0B for chicken claims.

According to recent reports, for chicken, 2027 is the key year. Summary judgment briefing finishes in March 2027 and trial is scheduled for September 2027. The larger settlements usually come after the summary judgment ruling and before the trial.

Burford will not comment on individual cases and discourages investors from trying to underwrite them: âwe always encourage investors to restrict their underwriting process to reach an investment decision to the data and inputs for the portfolio as a whole, not individual assets.â The company is not spoon-feeding investors anything.

Sources indicate that we have shared some of our work on the protein cases with sell-side analysts and a legal reporter with little effect so far. Everyone grasps the soundbite that the protein cases could return more than Burfordâs market cap, but proving it means reading dockets. There is no central record of settlements and opt-out amounts are confidential. The defendants donât want to talk about the cases either.

Recent findings suggest that however, one can build a bottom-up estimate of what chicken could pay. Tysonâs and Pilgrimâs filings disclose settlement expense, and PACER, bankruptcy filings, and SEC filings show who settled and when. Our estimates rely on several assumptions, so I donât want to overstate the precision, but I believe they are directionally correct.

Pilgrimâs pleaded guilty to price fixing and faces treble damages at trial, so it will likely settle for the most per dollar of purchases. Tysonâs cooperation with the Justice Department caps its damages at single damages, so it will logically pay less than Pilgrimâs Pride. The private producers, which admitted nothing, should settle as well. They have still paid well over $100M to the classes.

Burford holds at least $12B in qualified claims (purchaSes) from Sysco (SYY) and the bankruptcy claims of Maines Paper & Food Service. Damages experts in the case have estimated overcharges of roughly 8% to 22% depending on the period and product; a blend is about 11%, or about 33Â¢ per dollar after trebling. In theory, with treble damages, the Burford claims could be worth about $4B (about ), but the simplest way to think about the settlements is in terms of pennies on the dollar for purchases made.

According to recent reports, initial settlements in 2019â2022 were made for 1Â¢ or 2Â¢ on the dollar. As the case has progressed and trial has neared, the settlement rates seem to have gone up. In the most recent quarter, Pilgrimâs Pride settled with 13 claimants for what we estimate to be approximately 6.5Â¢ per dollar spent. There is one public data point for 8Â¢. Tyson has settled for 1Â¢ to 2Â¢ so far but may pay more as trial nears.

Our base case for settlements for just chicken in 2027 is $1.53 a share (before tax), which is material relative to Burfordâs current sub-$4 share price. The assumed settlement rates are 8Â¢ from Pilgrimâs, 4Â¢ from Tyson and 5.5Â¢ from the private producers. We have built a tool to allow you to play with the assumptions and see the status of settlements (link). The grid below shows how gross dollar settlements translate into per share amounts.Â³.

Recent findings suggest that everyone is motivated to settle. Burford's debt covenants make it hard to borrow for newly introduced cases, so chicken proceeds matter to its funding, and insiders own about 9%. The defendants, except Tyson, face trebled damages at trial, which is why these cases rarely go to trial. The clock is running, and I would be surprised if the chicken claims settle for less than historical rates in 2027.

Kingsway is building a organization around the search model, where it backs hungry, A-player operators, dropping them into undermanaged lifestyle businesses bought at around 5x EBITDA. As I wrote last quarter, the bogey to drive returns is "Double-digit organic growth, accelerating EBITDA, and additional acquisitions.".

On its earnings call, the manufacturer reaffirmed that it expects double-digit organic growth and 3-5 acquisitions this year. More importantly, it reported its best portfolio EBITDA in years: more than $7M for the quarter, or $28M annualized, compared to $22M over the previous 12 months.

It has been revealed that what could this tech giant look like in 12 months? Start with the $28M run-rate EBITDA and grow it 20% from a combination of organic growth (guided to 10% or more), acquisitions, and operating leverage, and there is a legitimate path to $33M+ of portfolio EBITDA at the end of 2027. Subtract $5M of corporate expense, apply a 20x multiple, deduct net debt ($62M) and preferred shares ($16.3M), and you get an equity value of more than $16 per share. The 20x multiple is not as rich as it sounds. The company pays effectively no taxes because of NOLs, and the businesses it owns are asset-light with minimal capex. A 20x multiple is not uncommon for growing serial acquirers, but it does imply continued organic growth and acquisitions.

Kingsway has no sell-side coverage and no earnings estimates, which makes it almost impossible for the computers to see. The steady pace of acquisitions and the GAAP accounting adjustments required for its warranty business obscure the picture further. The machines may not be looking, but the engine is working: organic growth, accelerating EBITDA, and acquisitions, driven by aligned incentives and a hungry group of A-player managers whose backgrounds include U.S. military academies, relevant work experience, and top tier MBAs. Insiders own roughly 60% of the manufacturer, and a new board chair is committed to engaging the capital markets and telling the investment story.

Over the next year, organic growth, acquisitions and the divestiture of a legacy business could produce strong results and make Kingsway self-funding and GAAP profitable. That would make it attractive to a larger set of human and computer buyers.

Hagerty had a strong start to the year, raised full-year earnings guidance, and is making progress toward fulfilling our thesis that "operating leverage returns and results beat consensus estimates." The business is firing on all cylinders. In the first half, it added a record 279,000 latest members, grew written premium 19% year over year, and increased cash flow from operations 91% to $186M.

Industry observers note that the biggest fly in the ointment is a change in Hagerty's arrangement with Markel (MKL), which owns about 23% of the manufacturer. Under the revised "fronting" agreement, Hagerty makes more money (good), but GAAP accounting creates a one-year period where reported revenue declines (optically bad). The transitional charges shrink each quarter through 2026 and disappear in 2027, when year-over-year revenue comparisons will also reflect the latest accounting basis in both periods. In the meantime, the transition makes apples-to-apples year-over-year GAAP comparisons incredibly difficult. The Hagerty family owns almost half the company, is managing it for the long haul, and has tried to explain the long-term benefits. The progress is temporarily hidden from the computers, but the operating metrics are industry leading.

Hagerty's quarterly earnings are hard to predict because most of them come from auto insurance, where weather can swing results from year to year. We will likely avoid any Category 4 or 5 hurricane landfall in the continental U.S. in 2026 (good for people and good for earnings). The company can build and release reserves, so some of the benefit may show up in reserves rather than 2026 EPS, but it is unequivocally positive. The absence of Category 4 or 5 hurricanes and operational progress may allow accelerated earnings even in an investment year for Hagerty.

We are watching several things that few computers are tuned to: 1,000-page regulatory filings where one page matters, the number of states approving the State Farm program (now 42), online auction results for the Marketplace business (up 50% year over year), and the quiet expansion of the GEICO trial. In the meantime, I expect the company to "beat and raise" in one or both of the next two quarters and the impact on GAAP earnings of the changes to the Markel agreement to roll off.

According to recent reports, it is too early to tell if our short-term thesis on Cellebrite is correct: "Genesis generates meaningful revenue and Cellebrite begins to be viewed as an AI beneficiary." The product introduced at the end of the second quarter, and the company booked modest revenue and cited $1M in Genesis-related ARR. Between government procurement cycles and the many free trials Cellebrite is offering, there is not enough data on Genesis yet.

Industry observers note that on the less encouraging front, the CEO stepped down. The tech giant called it a planned transition, but several factors, including the cut to 2026 guidance from 18% ARR growth to 16% ARR growth, make me quite skeptical of the story that it was always planned. While the CEO's departure is not a positive, all the pieces still hold. Cellebrite operates in a near-duopoly selling mission-critical software to agencies with large budgets. The agencies are labor- and talent-constrained, and Cellebrite, with its Genesis offering, provides them with an opportunity for a step-function increase in productivity from their constrained labor pool. The new CEO is a "product" guy and is committed to building out the Cellebrite platform.

We searched public contracts for clues on Genesis adoption. The contracts are usually too opaque to show sales by product, so that was a dead end, but they were useful for tracking federal sales. The good news is that federal procurement awards appear to be up more than 20% year over year, a clear reacceleration. Federal is under 20% of the business, so it is not a full proxy for Cellebrite's revenue, but investors have focused on it since DOGE slowed it in 2025.

Organization disclosures over the next three quarters will tell us whether Genesis can boost organic growth. In the meantime, we will scour public agency procurements for evidence. We own a company with segment-leading technology, mid-teens growth, and a mid-teens P/E, with the potential to expand both.

According to recent reports, this is a newly introduced investment added last quarter. The manufacturer owns seven businesses and was built by issuing shares to buy businesses while paying management and incentive fees to an âexternalâ management company. Fraud at one of the portfolio companies, an accounting restatement, and too much debt proved too much for investors, and they fled.

Today, an activist is involved, one business has been sold, debt is coming down, and the restatement is behind the company. In round numbers, the shares traded at $11 at quarter end, and by my math the underlying assets are likely worth $30+ per share, but could be worth substantially more with some financial engineering. If you can sell assets, generate cash, and buy back shares at 30 cents on the dollar, the share count declines much more rapidly than the value of the remaining assets. Our thesis is âAssets are sold, shares are repurchased, and management is internalized.â.

Two things happened this past quarter that are encouraging. First, the incoming CEO mentioned, âWe are still highly committed to an additional divestiture in order to accelerate the deleveraging process... we are continuing to evaluate multiple opportunities.â He called it âan important part of the next stepsâ for closing the gap to intrinsic value. So management is aligned with at least part of our thesis.

Recent findings suggest that second, several board members finally bought shares in the open market, totaling about $1.7M. Even with those purchases, the board and the external manager own a comically small portion of the tech giant, and in my opinion they are very vulnerable to an activist taking control. I believe the purchases show the board sees an opportunity and would like to keep its seats, which will likely require asset sales and buybacks.

In my view, a proxy fight will likely occur in 2027 if the divestitures do not happen under the current board. Nominations for board members are due in January. The clock is ticking; the question should be who is on the board when the divestitures and buybacks happen, not whether they happen.

Much of the letter has been devoted to picking through filings and building a mosaic that eventually should become visible to the computers and the market. That paradigm does not apply to KKR, the alternative manager and one of the most widely covered financial companies in the world, where nothing is hidden. Below are some metrics from its most recent quarter:.

In a recent development, yet the shares are down more than 25% YTD. The metrics above are backward-looking, but many of the concerns about KKR are forward-looking. There is a lot of chatter about issues in private credit and retail investors wanting money back from semi-liquid vehicles. That is true, but also true is that the retail funds in question are less than 5% of AUM and KKR will very likely raise more private credit capital in 2026 than in any prior year. AUM is still growing.

In a recent development, A second knock on the alternative asset managers is that they are not monetizing assets or returning capital to their limited partners, leaving those limited partners with less capital to commit to future funds. Based on recent announcements, KKR is on pace to have record monetizations this year.

The share prices of the alternative managers have moved almost in lockstep.

Industry observers note that in my opinion, the lockstep decline is creating opportunities, because operating fundamentals and exposures to software, AI, and private credit vary by alternative manager. Even if you accept the industry headwinds as valid (I do not), we may end up owning another alternative manager with strong operating metrics and a valuation depressed by the same multiple compression.

Recent findings suggest that for KKR, the shares trade at approximately 13x consensus 2027 earnings. Ultimately I don't think this disconnect between fundamentals, operating performance, valuation and share price will persist. These businesses have operating leverage: as AUM goes up, earnings power goes up faster. Given the quantum of uncalled capital, fee paying AUM is going up. Unless the books are completely mismarked, earnings are going up too, and we are reaching the point where, absent a large geopolitical risk-off event, multiples should trough or even improve. A reversion to a market multiple plus continued growth would imply a return of more than 50% over the next 12 months.

According to recent reports, as part of reducing portfolio concentration, we rebought Liquidia after it lost the patent decision. Liquidia has reached a financially manageable settlement with United Therapeutics (UTHR) that clears all legal issues between the two.

We initiated a small new position in the AI basket. I am still not comfortable buying the first-order beneficiaries â chip manufacturers or power providers. We did, however, buy shares in Limbach, which should benefit from the unprecedented data center buildout.

Industry observers note that limbach designs, installs and maintains mechanical, electrical, plumbing and controls systems for commercial and institutional buildings. The core of the business is heating and air conditioning in complex facilities. Limbach bids on large, complicated projects such as hospitals and generally passes on simpler work like office buildings and warehouses. Its largest customer is the hospital operator HCA (HCA).

We owned Limbach several years ago but grew frustrated that nearly every quarter brought âone-timeâ charges that looked more routine than one-time. Back then, Limbach mostly worked as a subcontractor to general contractors. Since then, a new CEO has pushed the company toward work commissioned directly by building owners, and margins, profitability and predictability have all improved.

Industry observers note that in pursuing owner-direct work, Limbach largely passed on data centers. That was costly. Data center construction now absorbs a striking share of U.S. investment, and cooling is one of the central engineering problems in those buildings. Worse, data center builders are bidding up wages for exactly the skilled labor Limbach employs, squeezing its margins without bringing any of the revenue.

In the second quarter, Limbach stumbled. Gross margin fell from 28% to 21.5%, owner-direct organic revenue declined, and management cut its full-year EBITDA guidance by about 12%. The stock fell 35% the next day. Alongside the results, Limbach unveiled the acquisition of CYMCOR, a program manager for data center construction. The logic mirrors what Limbach did in healthcare, where its program management arm has steered roughly $60M of project work to Limbach while generating about $3M of program management fees. Limbach paid $30M, about 7.5x managementâs forecast of CYMCORâs 2027 EBITDA. The deal pays for itself only modestly on its own; the payoff comes if it opens doors to data center projects.

In a recent development, we bought our shares at roughly 12x this yearâs free cash flow. There are credible paths to grow both revenue and margins: the business normalizing as guidance assumes, plus upcoming data center work. If Limbach delivers on both, the multiple will likely expand too, and we would benefit three ways.

The bear case has the margin compression being permanent and the promised second-half growth not showing up. While I donât think this will happen, the shares could certainly go lower. Still, I believe the odds are skewed in our favor. The share price was more than double what we paid as recently as May, and peer multiples are nearly double Limbachâs. If Limbach is operationally successful, the share price should take care of itself.

It has been revealed that we ended the quarter short both Pilgrimâs Pride and Tyson Foods (TSN) given the potential magnitude of the settlement payments required to end their protein litigation. The companies appear to accrue for the settlement expenses as deals are signed. The potential liability is not a focus of investors as analysts rarely ask questions about the companiesâ pending litigation. Given the coming court dates, the magnitude of the settlements may surprise investors and negatively impact their share prices. We are also short a major index and a mature fast-food chain with challenged growth and a very healthy multiple.

We have done the work, we have the receipts. Time will tell if we get paid. The passage of time should be our friend. This quarter, we learn whether an overbid emerges for Lifecore. In early November, Limbach reports the quarter that tests its guidance. Nominations for Compass Diversified's board are due January 21, so we will learn soon if a group emerges to push for asset sales and buybacks. The AnaptysBio ruling should arrive in the first half of 2027. Over the next two quarters, the Markel accounting noise rolls off and Hagerty's GAAP numbers become useful again. Over the next three quarters, Cellebrite's traction with its Genesis product and ability to sustain growth will become clear. By the end of March, summary judgment briefing in chicken is complete, with a September 2027 trial pushing the chicken defendants toward settlement and bringing cash to Burford.

In a recent development, we will know if we are right or not; there will be results for the computers to see or not. Non-consensus will become consensus or not. Multiples can compress or expand. That is out of our control, but we know what we own and why we own it and look forward to the computers seeing what we see.

Recent findings suggest that while we do not have complete transparency into the holdings of the more than a dozen managers in the Partners Fund, we have a very good sense of each managerâs largest holdings. As North Peak Capital pointed out in their letter:.

Excerpt from North Peak Capital Q2 letter.

... within the S&P 500 year-to-date. Approximately 70% of the indexâs gains were driven by a mere 10 companies, all but one directly tied to the âAI trade.â Excluding those names, the remaining 490 companies â representing roughly 90% of the S&P 500âs aggregate revenue â have generated a ~3% return, compared to the indexâs 10% gain so far this year. Put another way, 2% of S&P companies drove 70% of the return, and on average, those companies more than tripled in value.

There are a number of ways to slice the data and categorize companies, but semiconductors and hyperscalers now represent a very substantial portion of the S&P 500âs market capitalization (30%+), and the exposure is larger still if other AI-related hardware and power companies are included (40%+).

It has been revealed that for better or worse, the Partners Fundâs returns were generated with very little benefit from the âAI trade.â I am highlighting this fact to help you contextualize your Partners Fund investment. The holdings are materially different from those of the large indices. While the Partners Fund, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq all own equities, the nature of those exposures is quite different. There are times when that will be âgood differentâ and times when that will be âbad different.â In general, the Partners Fund will hold smaller companies and have more international exposure than the large market indices.

In a recent development, nobody is disputing the utility of AI or the innovation that it will drive; it is certainly the âITâ fashion of the day, dominating market narratives. Again returning to the North Peak letter, I think their sentiment on the âAIâ stocks is similar to that of several managers within the Partners Fund.

Excerpt from North Peak Capital Q2 letter: AI stocks.

For AI stocks, we simply cannot circumscribe our assessments with a satisfactory degree of precision; they may be great investments, but they arenât great investments for us, given their inherent unpredictability and dynamism. In many instances, the moats are unusually unstable, because capabilities that looks proprietary in one quarter can be commoditized or leapfrogged by the next model release or next technological innovation.

Recent findings suggest that there is a scale and capital intensity to the AI buildout that has also given managers pause. Until recently, the Mag 7 businesses that absorbed capital were capital light and monopolistic in nature, rarely competing directly. The cumulative capital commitment to the AI buildout is measured in the trillions, debt is increasingly being issued to finance it, and the winners are not preordained.

I also want to highlight Bonsai Partnersâ recent investment in Constellation Software (CNSWF), which touches on the AI theme from the perspective of a tech giant many investors currently perceive as an AI âloser.â.

Excerpt from Bonsai Partners letter: Constellation Software.

Ultimately, I expect AI to widen the distribution of outcomes in software rather than move the entire sector in one direction. It will expose businesses whose apparent moat depended heavily on access to cheap capital or a more polished product, while potentially strengthening incumbents that control something rare and valuable that AI and competitors cannot easily copy. The broad selloff provides an opportunity because it has treated much of the sector indiscriminately, even though some companies may emerge as beneficiaries.

In the letter, Portfolio Manager Andrew Rosenblum touches on what attracted him to Constellation Software and the potential upside:.

Sources indicate that if the core investment case remains intact, we will have the privilege of owning a durable collection of mission-critical businesses at a rational starting price, supported by an unusual capital-allocation culture and a long runway for compounding. That combination is rare, and when uncertainty created the opportunity earlier this year, I moved decisively to make us part owners of Constellation... Thinking about upside scenarios, if the company fully deploys its free cash flow while maintaining its investment hurdle rates, reinvestment alone could sustain a compounded growth rate of roughly 20%, consistent with the companyâs history. Its existing businesses could also continue to generate low- to mid-single-digit profit growth, as they have in the past, with incremental revenue gains or cost savings from AI providing further upside. As always, these are scenarios rather than forecasts, but the building blocks suggest that a 20% to 25% free cash flow CAGR is a realistic possibility, even though our baseline remains a more conservative 15% to preserve a margin of error.

Recent findings suggest that not every source of return in the Partners Fund is a multi-year holding, and managers do have the flexibility to invest in the largest companies. Maran Capital found a short-lived mispricing around the SpaceX (SPCX) IPO in June that illustrates the type of opportunity a small, nimble manager can take advantage of:.

Excerpt from Maran Capital Q2 letter: SpaceX.

Recent findings suggest that in late May, I discovered a mutual fund that had a large position in SpaceX... This fund was carrying SpaceX at a valuation of $1.25 trillion (approximately $105 per share), the level of SpaceX's last fundraising round. SpaceX was slated to go public less than two weeks later at a $1.75 trillion valuation ($135 per share). I wouldn't have invested in the SpaceX IPO at a $1.75 trillion valuation... But at $1.25 trillionâan almost 30% discount to the IPO priceâit was a very different proposition... We purchased shares of the fund and hedged out, as best we could, its portfolio of stocks other than SpaceX... On June 12, SpaceX did indeed IPO at a $1.75 trillion valuation... We had our hedged trade on for approximately two weeks and generated a healthy return with what I believe was de minimis risk. This was as close to 'free alpha' as we have discovered in the market in recent years... The trade was asymmetric, had a large margin of safety, was liquid, and was uncorrelated.".

I end each letter saying our fund of funds is going to be different. It will be smaller, the underlying holdings will be more esoteric, and I hope the managers will continue to collaborate more over time. I believe that it will be "good different, " but only time will tell. Thank you for joining me on this journey. I will work hard to grow your family's capital alongside mine.

The Ultimate Life Coach

📅 18 May 2024 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2073 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Almost  nineteen years into early retirement now, I’ve come to realize that the complete freedom of this lifestyle can be a double-edged sword.
  • It has been revealed that you’ve already heard me raving plenty about the upside: having the freedom to raise a son from the day he was born to beyond his eighteenth birthday with no compromises.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Almost  nineteen years into early retirement now, I’ve come to realize that the complete freedom of this lifestyle can be a double-edged sword.

It has been revealed that you’ve already heard me raving plenty about the upside: having the freedom to raise a son from the day he was born to beyond his eighteenth birthday with no compromises. And then to put thousands of hours into everything else I value as well: family, health, friends, adventures, building stuff, and even writing the occasional blog post. No complaints about any of this.

But if I can indulge you to play me a brief Tiny Violin of First World Problems solo, even this perfect life comes with one flaw: I never have to do anything I don’t want to do.

According to recent reports, to most people, this sounds like a dream come true. Especially if you combine total freedom with plenty of money, life is just a non-stop blissful playground of self actualization, right?

It has been revealed that well, maybe, but maybe not. In reality, the answer depends on who you are.

Freedom and money reveal a person’s true strengths and weaknesses, and the result is a spectrum with “Unlimited drugs and booze on the couch” at one end, and “Create and manage a series of nonprofit foundations which employ thousands of people to research and invest in medical advances and clean energy” at the other.

According to recent reports, for most of my journey so far, I seem to have found the balance pretty naturally. My Dad job was very intense for the first decade, but somehow I also had time to build and restore quite a few houses in the neighborhood, take plenty of intense trips to interesting places, give some talks and make some videos, and still write a few hundred blog posts.

But in these last few years, I have started slowing down, and it has become more and more difficult to wrangle and focus myself to get these things to happen as often.

Instead of constantly bouncing around the construction site building cool things, or falling into laser focus on the keyboard finishing an article that I just had to share with you, I found myself retiring to the couch earlier and earlier each afternoon, seeking distraction on the phone and wishing I had the energy and focus to do those other more enjoyable things.

It has been revealed that so I fought back, by learning more about health and wellness. Trying to study and train my way into more energy and focus and motivation. And you’ve seen some of the results here, in articles I’ve shared about daily habits, steering clear of excessive comfort, and more.

Sources indicate that and all of these things really work, IF you take the knowledge and actually put it into action. And therein lies the problem:.

I kept learning effective newly introduced things, and successfully incorporating them into my life. They would work for a while, but gradually my brain would invent various excuses to stop doing them consistently, leaving me with plenty of knowledge but far too little accomplishment to show for it.

Until finally, just a few months ago, I realized that I had been sabotaging my own progress by turning my biggest life advantage into a disadvantage:.

I have been using my freedom too much – in order to avoid doing things that I didn’t feel like doing.

See, freedom is great if it frees you from leaving your children at 5am so you can drive an hour through a traffic jam to sit in an office building for nine hours. But that same freedom goes to waste if you then just plunk the kids down in front of a playlist of cheap cartoons while you lounge in the corner to scroll Facebook all day.

You need to use it to do things that are even more valuable than the job you just quit. And if you can’t do that, you might as well just keep the damned job.

Sources indicate that this is what I was doing, while lying about it to myself. I would focus on the easy things which are still good for me, like taking care of the house or hanging out with friends who live nearby. But I avoid doing the harder things – which for me means the things that require more planning, energy or focus. Even though these are the things that allow me to lead the life I enjoy most.

Let’s use workouts as an easy example. I already know that on a minute-for-minute basis, this is the single most effective thing almost anybody can do with their time because it drastically improves every other area of life. But despite knowing this, I was still following this pattern:.

“I want to get in a really good weight training workout today.But I don’t feel like doing a workout because it’s hard.So I’ll try to grease the wheels for myself so it’s easier to achieve. I’ll pick the perfect time of day when the weather is nice, and my energy level is high. I’ll set up my gym in advance the night before.And when that golden moment of perfect conditions hits,I’ll hit the gym!“.

But between you and me, that moment didn’t always come. Some weeks I’d achieve it 2-3 times, some weeks I’d get “busy” and make excuses like “well at least I walked a lot today”. Some days I would complete a great workout, but when recording it in the journal I’d see that the previous one was over a week ago.

And the results of this lackluster effort were exactly what you’d expect: lackluster fitness.

Then something changed and I learned that there’s a much better way to get those workouts done. It’s by replacing the long, meandering, frankly wussypants dialog above with this one:.

According to recent reports, I want to work out today.I don’t feel like it.^^^ AHA!! I JUST CAUGHT MYSELF TRYING TO SELF SABOTAGE! ^^^I am now already putting on my shoes and walking to the gym.

I’m using workouts as an example because this is the behavior I managed to change most successfully, but the exact same technique applies to everything else that you or I want to do, but fail to do regularly.

The key is learning to watch over yourself like an Eagle and identify that exact moment of hesitation.

And then instead of using it as a trigger for excuses, you use it as a trigger for action.

Industry observers note that it’s so counterintuitive at first, but then obvious in retrospect. Hesitance feels shitty in the moment, and it really can ruin your life if you listen to it too often. But the ultimate solution is usually to run directly towards, rather than away from, the stuff you don’t want to do.

So really, Hesitation can be the ultimate life coach.

Using Extremely Badass People as Fuel.

As part of writing this article, I shared the idea around with friends to test it out first. And I was initially surprised to get mixed results. About half of them could relate with me: they felt they were underachieving in life and wanted to do more. The other half though I was crazy: these people feel they are already doing too much, raising multiple kids and managing multiple businesses and training for ironman triathlons in the mountains.

The overachievers go through life nicely buzzed but often stressed. When hearing them describe their schedules, I was absolutely not envious. At the same time, they weren’t impressed with my schedule either because it’s too easy. We could both benefit from making adjustments towards the center.

Impressive overachiever friends are one thing, but the thing that really flipped the switch for me was hearing a podcast interview with our planet’s most extreme example of driving yourself beyond your former limits, David Goggins.

Sources indicate that I learned about his life story with a mix of awe and horror. Severely beaten as a child, he grew up with a looming wall of psychological demons and issues, but his reaction was the unique part: he has been driven to compulsively seek out and overcome extreme hardship, not just to unimaginable levels but hundreds of times beyond that.

From pushing through several near-death experiences just to qualify for a Navy SEALS career, to breaking his own legs, heart and lungs from the constant exertion of things like running 240 miles over four days without sleeping, to setting a world record of 4025 bar pull ups over 24 hours (shredding his hands to look like ground beef in the process), the man does things I would never have thought are even close to possible for a human.

And that flipped a switch for me, by putting my own incredibly easy, under-achieving life into perspective.

Because while I absolutely do not want any part of the Goggins life, and I would gladly live my life never having run more than 10 miles at a single stretch, I do find it incredibly helpful to learn that pretty much all of our barriers are entirely mental, not physical or placed upon us by the outside world.

Sure, we do have different starting points and different amounts of luck. But instead of thinking of life like this:.

I now realize that things are more like this:.

And that’s a really empowering way to think about life, that feels like the sky has opened way up.

Recent findings suggest that so the podcast was just an introduction. I wrote down the particularly concise quote “You already fuckin’ know what to do.” on a piece of cardstock, stuck it to my bathroom mirror, and started acting on it immediately.

Suddenly, I was able to hit the gym every single day because I had two ways to approach it: wanting to put in a workout, and not wanting to put in a workout, either of which became a trigger to work out immediately.

It has been revealed that and of course, once I finally put in the effort, it started working. Even though I’ve been sorta into this type of training since I was a teenager, I have mostly floated along on a plateau for years. But with this change in attitude, I gained ten pounds of lean weight over the first four months, returning to the strength and flexibility that I had at age 25, and every single joint in my body feels like it has been upgraded to a study, well oiled spring.

In a recent development, I also used the “catch yourself at the moment of hesitance” trick to get myself to run instead of walk more often (over 20 runs since I got back to Colorado last month), get over to the MMM-HQ coworking space for more work and socializing visits, and even to sit back down at the computer to write this post for you. While I’ve found that too much blogger work (and internet “success”) is a bad thing, there is still a right level that works for me. But it takes a lot of discipline to be willing to do it, because of all the other easier and more thrilling activities I could be doing with this same stretch of time.

In a recent development, for me, fully internalizing this one powerful piece of inspiring profanity has been transformative. But I still find that returning regularly to the well makes all this work even better. So I downloaded both of the Goggins audiobooks and worked through them in little chunks on my morning walks over the period of a month. Then I moved on to Peter Attia’s Outlive, and Jocko Willink’s Extreme Ownership.

While the intellectuals fret about the perils of “Bro Science” or the “Toxic Masculinity” of today’s tribe of health podcasters and question their motivation, I simply absorb the messages that work for me and discard the rest. Find people who make you reach a little higher, and feed on their energy.

Sources indicate that and for me, being exposed to successful, strong, athletic people who squeeze a lot of work out of themselves is a big source of inspiration. It helps me do more with my day, which is exactly what works for me right now at this phase of life.

And I wish you more of what works for you too!

6 Best Subscription Management Apps (To Cancel Recurring Transactions)

📅 11 Jan 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (774 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Wellkeptwallet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Managing your money isn’t just about earning more.
  • Before choosing an app, know what features matter most:.
  • Rocket Money is one of the most well-known subscription managers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Managing your money isn’t just about earning more. It’s also about stopping unnecessary losses. In today’s digital economy, recurring subscription charges (streaming services, premium apps, trials, memberships) quietly drain money each month. Most people spend hundreds, or even thousands, annually on services they don’t use. Subscription manager apps help you see recurring charges, track billing cycles, and cancel those you no longer want.

Before choosing an app, know what features matter most:.

Rocket Money is one of the most well-known subscription managers. It scans your linked bank and credit accounts for recurring charges and displays them on a clear dashboard. People like it for its ability to detect subscriptions and assist with cancellations directly in the app, a major time-saver for busy people.

Why it stands out• Automatically detects recurring payments• Lets you cancel unwanted subscriptions directly from the app• Includes extra budgeting tools and spending alerts• Trusted security with read-only bank access.

Who it’s for: People who want the fastest way to spot and stop unwanted recurring charges without manually entering every service.

Trim is another financial assistant that scans transactions and flags recurring charges. While subscription tracking is a smaller part of its feature set, it also provides bill negotiation support and money-saving alerts. Many customers like Trim because it reaches out on your behalf about subscriptions via text or in-app messaging.

Why it stands out• Recurring transaction detection• Alerts about unusual subscriptions or trials converting to paid• Bill negotiation tools beyond basic subscription tracking.

Who it’s for: Users who want automation plus help reducing bills and optimizing spending.

PocketGuard is primarily a budgeting app that includes subscription tracking as part of a broader financial overview. Instead of being solely a subscription manager, it integrates recurring expenses into your overall budget, helping you get a full picture of your finances.

Why it stands out• Syncs automatically with financial accounts• Highlights recurring expenses in the context of your whole budget• Helps track cash flow and affordability.

Who it’s for: People who want subscriptions tracked inside a complete personal finance dashboard.

Monarch Money offers robust financial planning tools: budgets, goals, net worth tracking, and more, with subscription visibility included in the package. Owners often choose it for its highly customizable interface and deep analytics. It’s not subscription-only, but it gives you full clarity on recurring expenses as part of larger planning.

Why it stands out• Powerful budgeting + subscription tracking.• Clean, customizable data visuals.• Goal-based money management.

Who it’s for: Customers who want subscription insights in the context of total financial planning — and who are okay paying for premium features.

If you don’t want to link bank accounts, Bobby is a lightweight subscription tracker that lets you manually enter each subscription, along with billing dates and amounts. It then sends reminders so you don’t forget renewals. It’s simple, privacy-friendly, and great for a hands-on approach.

Why it stands out• No bank/credit card linking required.• Clean and minimal interface.• Calendar views and notification reminders.

Who it’s for: Privacy-focused customers or those who prefer full manual control.

Industry observers note that subby offers functionality similar to Bobby’s but is known for integrations and subscription reminders tailored for Android owners. It lets you manually track expenses with flexible billing schedules and alerts. (While not all resources list Subby as a top pick, it’s frequently mentioned among good manual trackers.).

Why it stands out• Manual entry with customizable notifications.• Good choice for Android users.

Who it’s for: People who want a simple manual tracker without linking financial accounts.

If you’d rather not use a third-party app at all, both Apple and Google offer direct subscription management:.

iPhone (Apple Subscriptions):Settings → Your Name → Subscriptions → Select subscription → Cancel Subscription.

Android (Google Play):Open Google Play → Subscriptions → Select subscription → Cancel subscription.

These built-in tools won’t automatically find all recurring charges if some are billed outside the app stores, but they are a secure and effective way to manage many mobile subscriptions.

Here’s a quick guide based on what matters most to you:.

You can also combine approaches — use a subscription app plus your budgeting system to spot recurring leaks and strategy better for annual vs monthly charges.

Industry observers note that subscription manager apps help plug the leaks in your financial bucket, so more of your hard-earned money stays where it belongs: with you. Whether you want automatic detection and help with cancellations, a full financial overview, or full privacy with manual entry, there’s an option that fits your style. Explore one or two subscription manager apps that align with your priorities, and don’t forget to check your finances regularly.

Sources indicate that A living trust is a legal arrangement where you (the grantor) transfer ownership of your assets to a trust entity that you also control (as trustee). It sounds circular, and in practice, during your lifetime, nothing changes about how you use your money and property. The magic happens when you die or become incapacitated.

The three key roles in a living trust:.

During your lifetime: You are both the grantor and the trustee. You control everything. You can add or remove assets, change beneficiaries, modify terms, or dissolve the trust entirely. Your Social Security number is the trust's tax ID — there is no separate tax return. For practical purposes, nothing changes about your daily financial life.

Recent findings suggest that if you become incapacitated: Your successor trustee immediately takes over management of trust assets. No court petition needed. No guardianship proceeding. No delay. This is a major advantage over a will, which provides zero protection during incapacity.

When you die: Your successor trustee distributes assets according to your trust document. No probate court. No public record. No waiting 6-18 months. Beneficiaries can typically receive assets within days or weeks.

Industry observers note that A living trust essentially creates a private, self-executing transfer system that operates outside the court system entirely. For FI families who have spent years building wealth, this means your heirs receive the full value of your estate without probate eating into it.

The terms "revocable" and "irrevocable" describe whether you can change or dissolve the trust after creating it. This distinction has major implications for control, taxes, and asset protection.

Revocable living trust — the standard choice for most families:.

You retain full control. You can amend the trust, add or remove assets, change beneficiaries, or dissolve it completely at any time. Because you maintain control, the IRS treats trust assets as yours — they are included in your taxable estate, and creditors can reach them. The primary benefit is probate avoidance and incapacity protection, not asset protection or tax reduction.

Irrevocable trust — the advanced tool for specific situations:.

Once created, you generally cannot change or revoke it. You give up control of the assets placed inside. In exchange, you get benefits that a revocable trust cannot provide.

When an irrevocable trust makes sense:.

For most FI families: A revocable living trust is the right starting point. It provides the two biggest benefits — probate avoidance and incapacity protection — while letting you maintain complete control.

Creating a trust document is only half the job. A trust only controls assets that are titled in its name. An unfunded trust is a worthless piece of paper.

Assets you should transfer into your trust:.

Assets you should NOT put in your trust:.

The re-titling process for real estate: This is the most critical step and requires recording a latest deed. You transfer ownership from "John Smith" to "John Smith, Trustee of the John Smith Revocable Living Trust dated January 15, 2024." Contact your county recorder's office or have your attorney prepare the deed. Most counties charge $15-$75 for recording. Notify your mortgage firm (they cannot call the loan due under the Garn-St. Germain Act for transfers to a revocable trust) and your homeowners insurance carrier.

Ongoing funding discipline: Every time you open a latest bank account, buy property, or acquire significant assets, ask: "Should this be titled in my trust?" Create a simple checklist and review it annually. The most common estate planning failure is a perfectly drafted trust with assets still titled in the grantor's personal name.

A common concern is whether transferring your home into a trust triggers a due-on-sale clause in your mortgage. Under the federal Garn-St. Germain Depository Institutions Act of 1982, lenders cannot accelerate a mortgage when property is transferred to a revocable trust where the borrower remains a beneficiary and occupant. This protection applies to residential properties with fewer than five units. Your lender may ask for a copy of the trust document, but they cannot call the loan. Always notify your homeowners insurance company of the title change to ensure coverage remains valid.

According to recent reports, A living trust is most valuable if your net worth exceeds $500K, you own property in multiple states, you want to avoid probate, or you want incapacity protection. If your estate is simple and under $500K, a will may be sufficient.

It has been revealed that online services (Trust & Will $399-$599, LegalZoom $399-$599) work for simple trusts. For complex situations or estates over $1M, an estate planning attorney ($1,500-$5,000) ensures proper drafting and funding.

Industry observers note that your trust document should name your trustee (you), successor trustee, beneficiaries, and detailed distribution instructions. Include provisions for incapacity and specific instructions for each major asset category.

Transfer real estate by recording fresh deeds. Retitle bank and brokerage accounts into the trust name. Complete the assignment of personal property document. This is the most critical step — an unfunded trust is useless.

Draft a pour-over will that directs any assets not in the trust to pour into it upon your death. This will also names guardians for minor children. Review and update both documents every 3-5 years.

Sources indicate that A living trust is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. You serve as trustee and maintain full control. When you die or become incapacitated, a successor trustee you named manages and distributes assets to your beneficiaries — without probate or court involvement.

It has been revealed that A revocable living trust costs $1,500-$3,000 through an estate planning attorney, or $399-$599 through online services like Trust & Will or LegalZoom. Irrevocable trusts cost $3,000-$10,000+ due to their complexity. Additional costs include deed preparation ($200-$500) for transferring real estate.

A revocable living trust does NOT reduce estate taxes — assets are still part of your taxable estate because you maintain control. Only irrevocable trusts remove assets from your taxable estate. However, with the federal estate tax exemption at $13.61 million per individual (2024), estate taxes only affect very large estates.

Sources indicate that yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as your own trustee during your lifetime. You maintain complete control over all trust assets — buying, selling, spending, and investing exactly as you did before. Your successor trustee only takes over upon your death or incapacity.

Recent findings suggest that A will goes through probate court (public, 6-18 months, costs 3-7% of estate). A living trust avoids probate entirely (private, days to weeks, minimal cost). A trust also provides incapacity protection, which a will does not. However, a will can name guardians for minor children, which a trust cannot.

Yes. You need a pour-over will to catch any assets not titled in the trust and to name guardians for minor children. The trust handles your major assets and avoids probate. The will serves as a safety net for everything else.

A living trust is one of the most effective tools for protecting the wealth you have built on the path to financial independence. It avoids probate, provides incapacity protection, maintains complete privacy, and ensures your heirs receive assets rapidly and efficiently. The key is actually funding the trust — transferring asset titles into it. For FI families with a net worth above $500K, the $1,500-$5,000 setup cost pays for itself many times over in avoided probate fees and time savings for your heirs.

Sources indicate that managing money as a household is harder than it looks. Most people use a regular checking account at a significant bank, then juggle a separate budgeting app, maybe a savings account somewhere else, and possibly a kids’ debit card on top of that. It’s a lot to keep track of.

Crew is a fintech app that tries to put all of that in one place. It combines a high-yield checking account, built-in budgeting tools, and family banking features – all inside a single app. The goal is to help you organize your money, automate your budget, and earn more interest without switching between apps.

In this Crew review, we cover what it is, how it works, who it’s best for, the key features, pricing, and what real people are saying. If you’re looking for a smarter checking account that does more, this review gives you the full picture.

Crew is a fintech app that tries to put all of that in one place. It combines a high-yield checking account, built-in budgeting tools, and family banking features.

It has been revealed that crew is a financial technology (fintech) tech giant based in Lehi, Utah. It was founded by Gentry Davies and Steve Domino, who previously worked at Divvy, a business expense platform acquired by Bill.com. The app launched publicly and has been growing steadily since 2023.

Crew is not a bank. Banking services are provided by Bangor Savings Bank, which is FDIC-insured. Your deposits are held at Bangor Savings Bank, so they are protected up to federal insurance limits – $250,000 for individual accounts and $500,000 for joint accounts.

According to recent reports, the app is available on both iOS and Android. A web app is presently in beta.

Crew offers a checking account that earns 2.95% APY on your full balance. This rate applies to every dollar you hold in the account – there’s no minimum deposit requirement and no tiered rate structure.

According to recent reports, why it matters: Most big bank checking accounts pay close to 0.01% APY. Earning nearly 3% on your everyday checking balance can add meaningful interest over time, especially for families keeping a few thousand dollars in their account at any given time.

Pockets are virtual “buckets” inside your single Crew checking account. You can create as many as you need – for example, one for bills, one for savings, one for a vacation fund, one for groceries.

Why it matters: You don’t need a separate savings account or multiple bank accounts. Pockets let you visually and mentally divide your money without moving it to another institution. You can also lock a pocket in “piggy bank mode” to avoid dipping into it.

In a recent development, crew’s Autopilot feature lets you create rules that move money automatically based on triggers. Triggers can be events like a paycheck arriving or a balance dropping below a set level, or they can be time-based, like every Friday or the 1st of the month.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: Automation removes the discipline requirement from budgeting. You set your rules once, and Crew handles the rest. For example, you can tell Crew to automatically send 10% of every paycheck to your giving pocket, $500 to bills, and keep the rest in checking — without touching the app every payday.

Why it matters: Most banking apps bolt on a kid’s account as an afterthought. Crew builds family banking into the core experience. Parents get real-time spending notifications, spend controls, and the ability to set automated allowances.

Recent findings suggest that parents can set up automatic recurring transfers to a child’s account. You define the amount and the schedule, and Crew handles the delivery.

Why it matters: Automated allowances teach kids about money while removing the “I forgot to pay your allowance” problem for parents. Kids learn what consistent saving looks like in practice.

Every account member gets a Mastercard debit card. You can switch which pocket your card draws from at any time inside the app – or enhancement a transaction after the fact if you accidentally spent from the wrong pocket.

Why it matters: This setup means budgeting is “baked in” to your spending. Instead of tracking what you spent after the fact, you decide which budget category you’re spending from before or at the time of purchase.

Sources indicate that you can use your Crew Mastercard at any ATM in the Mastercard, Maestro, or Cirrus networks. Crew does not have its own fee-free ATM network, but it reimburses ATM fees for up to 20 withdrawals per year.

Why it matters: The annual ATM fee reimbursement covers most casual cash users without adding much complexity.

Crew supports outgoing wire transfers. The fee depends on your total account balance.

Incoming wires and standard ACH transfers are processed as usual through the app.

It has been revealed that no. Crew is a financial technology organization, not a bank. Banking services are provided by Bangor Savings Bank, Member FDIC, which is a real, federally insured bank. Your deposits are held at Bangor Savings Bank, so they are FDIC insured up to federal limits.

The APY is variable, meaning it can change over time. It is not a limited-time promotional rate in the traditional sense; it applies to your full balance, with no minimum or expiration. However, Crew can adjust the rate when market conditions change. The rate has fluctuated over the app’s history (it was as high as 3.7% in early 2025). Referral sign-ups may qualify for a 0.5% APY boost for the first three months.

Cash deposit support has been in development. Some reviews noted it was not yet available at the time of writing, though the feature has been in the works. It’s worth checking the current app version or Crew’s website for the latest on cash deposits before signing up if this is vital to you.

Industry observers note that you need your legal name, date of birth, physical address, and a tax ID (typically your Social Security number). Most applicants complete the process in under two minutes.

Sources indicate that crew earns revenue in two ways: from the interest it earns on deposits held at Bangor Savings Bank, and from merchant fees when you use your Crew debit card to make purchases. This model is common among fintech companies and allows them to offer no-fee accounts while still generating revenue.

User feedback for Crew is largely positive, particularly among families and people who value built-in budgeting features.

Rating: 4.8 out of 5 stars (based on 179 reviews as of March 2026).

Positive trends from Google Play owners include:.

Common critical feedback includes:.

Crew’s iOS app carries consistently high ratings. Consumers describe it as well-designed and easy to navigate. Family features are frequently praised, with parents noting that kids enjoy having their own card and app login.

Reviewers across platforms repeatedly mention Crew as a genuine alternative to maintaining separate banking and budgeting apps. The combination of high-yield checking, automatic paycheck splitting, and child accounts in one place is the most-cited reason for switching from other banks or apps.

The most consistent piece of constructive feedback is that Crew is still a young product and some features – like the web app – are still catching up to the mobile experience.

Crew is a well-designed fintech product that combines several things that usually require multiple apps or accounts: a high-yield checking account, budgeting through pockets, spending automation, and family banking.

Overall, Crew fills a genuine gap. Most checking accounts don’t pay meaningful interest and don’t have built-in budgeting. Crew does both, and it adds family banking on top. For households looking to simplify their financial toolkit and earn more interest on everyday balances, it’s worth a serious look.

As always, make sure to read the deposit agreement and check the current APY at trycrew.com before opening an account, since rates are variable and can change.

Recent findings suggest that this review is for informational purposes only and does not constitute financial advice. APY rates, fees, and features are subject to change. Always verify current terms directly with Crew at trycrew.com before making any financial decisions.

It has been revealed that debbie is a debt payoff app built around a truth most people already understand but rarely see addressed in finance tools: paying off debt is not just about numbers, it is about behavior. And if behavior is the real challenge, motivation matters more than spreadsheets.

That is where Debbie stands out.

Most personal finance apps track balances and interest rates and then stop there. Debbie goes a step further by rewarding people for making progress. When you do the right things consistently, you do not just see your debt go down. You actually get something back.

Many debt payoff journeys fail in the same place. Not at the beginning, when motivation is high, but in the middle, when progress feels slow, and life gets in the way. Debbie is designed specifically for that phase.

In a recent development, after connecting your credit cards, student loans, or other debts, the app creates a personalized payoff blueprint based on your balances and payment history. The plan is realistic and focused on consistency rather than extreme sacrifices.

As you make payments and reduce balances, Debbie rewards you for that progress.

Rewards can include things like:.

• Cash rewards• Gift cards• Partner offers tied to financial milestones.

In a recent development, these rewards are not meant to eliminate debt on their own. They exist to reinforce the habit of showing up and sticking with the proposal.

Debbie gives users a clean dashboard showing:.

This reduces the mental stress of juggling multiple accounts.

Unlike most personal finance apps, Debbie pays users for progress, which helps reinforce positive habits. Over $2,319,961.65 earned by people reaching their money goals.

The app is intentionally designed to be:.

This makes it beginner-friendly, even for people new to budgeting or debt payoff.

Recent findings suggest that debbie works best for people who need accountability and encouragement. If you already know what to do but struggle to stay consistent, this app fills an crucial gap.

• Rewards that reinforce good financial behavior• A clean, easy to understand interface• A focus on progress instead of perfection• Motivation during the hardest part of the journey.

There are also a few limitations to keep in mind. Debbie is not a replacement for a full budgeting system, and the rewards alone will not move the needle if you are carrying very large balances. You still have to do the work. The app simply makes it easier to keep going.

You will also need to link your financial accounts, which is standard for most modern finance apps but worth noting.

Debbie is a strong fit for people who feel overwhelmed by debt, burned out on traditional budgeting apps, or frustrated that they are doing the right things but still don’t feel any momentum.

According to recent reports, if you are already highly disciplined and managing everything with detailed spreadsheets, you may not need the additional reinforcement. For most people, though, motivation is the missing piece.

Yes. Debbie is a legitimate personal finance app built around a behavior-driven debt payoff model. While it won’t magically erase debt, it helps customers stay engaged, which is often the biggest missing piece in successfully paying off debt.

If you’re exploring Debbie, there are several other financial wellness and money-saving apps worth considering. Each app offers a different approach to helping owners improve their finances, build better habits, or earn rewards.

According to recent reports, acorns automatically invests your spare change by rounding up purchases to the nearest dollar. It’s designed for beginners who want a simple, hands-off way to start investing.

In a recent development, rocket Money focuses on budgeting, subscription tracking, and lowering monthly bills. It can help people identify recurring charges and negotiate certain expenses on their behalf.

Qapital combines budgeting with automated savings goals. Users can create custom “rules” that move money into savings automatically based on spending habits or milestones.

YNAB is a budgeting app built around giving every dollar a purpose. It’s popular among people who want a more hands-on system for managing cash flow and paying off debt.

In a recent development, paying off debt is rarely about knowledge. Most people already know what they should be doing. The real challenge is sticking with the initiative month after month, even when progress feels slow.

Debbie helps solve that problem by rewarding progress, reinforcing positive habits, and making the journey feel less discouraging. It will not magically erase debt. But it can absolutely help you stay consistent long enough to change your financial life.
